item.title: Dani Watt, wife of Steelers star T.J. Watt, questions NFL plan for Paris game
item.description: The NFL’s plans to stage a game in France amid protests in the country are being met with resistance from one of the most famous families in football.
item.content:encoded:
It appears the NFL’s plans to move forward with staging its first-ever regular season game in France are meeting resistance from one of the most famous families in football 

Dani Watt, wife of Pittsburgh Steelers star T.J. Watt, spoke out about the team’s NFL Week 7 matchup with the New Orleans Saints at Stade de France near Paris in an Instagram post Oct. 20. 

The country has been dealing with disruptive protests for several weeks, and they are continuing into the days immediately leading up to the game. 

Required reading: Steelers 'excited' for NFL Paris game vs Saints despite spate of disruptive protests

“Tell me how this one makes sense???” Watt wrote while linking to a report from a local CBS affiliate that explained the NFL’s plans to proceed despite the anti-government demonstrations that have frequently devolved into riots. 

T.J. Watt and the Steelers plan to depart the United States on Thursday. Coach Mike McCarthy said Monday that the full team met with officials from the league office to explain precautions and protocols that are in place to navigate the situation. He called it a “good plan” and described the team’s mood ahead of the matchup as “excited.”

The Steelers also chose to leave later in the week for their international game in Dublin, Ireland, last season. 

The Saints have been in France since early in the week, and there have been no reports of safety issues for them so far. 

Thousands have been arrested and some curfews have been enforced in areas in and around Paris as government officials attempt to restore order. Some of the protests have gripped Saint-Denis, a northern suburb of the city where Stade de France is located. 

The NFL has nevertheless told the public that league sites – including Stade de France – are secure. The stadium was previously the main track and field venue for the 2024 Olympics.

“We’re confident in our operational and security plans,” NFL vice president for international and club business Peter O’Reilly said during the league’s fall meeting Tuesday, Oct. 20.

The NFL is working in close partnership with security at Stade de France, which was the focal point of the Olympics in the city, O'Reilly said.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Dani Watt, wife of Steelers star T.J. Watt, questions NFL plan for Paris game

item.title: Jordan Elliott released by Titans after firearm incident. Here’s what we know
item.description: A Titans teammate reportedly had to stop Jordan Elliott from getting a gun.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans released veteran defensive tackle Jordan Elliot on Tuesday without offering much information. Details finally emerged over the course of Tuesday evening, and the situation is wilder than we can possibly imagine. Not only did Elliott threaten a teammate, but another player intervened to talk Elliott out of going to his vehicle and retrieving a firearm — which he presumably planned to return to the locker room with, either to threaten another player, or worse.

The first statement from the Titans did very little to explain what occurred. At first glance it reads more like some beef on the practice field led to a fight in the locker room, but it intentionally chose to gloss over the severity of what actually happened.

The statement is technically accurate, though most people would agree that there is a chasm of difference between “an incident at our team facility” and “he was going to his car to get a gun, potentially coming back to shoot someone.”

Here’s what we know from reports about the alleged situation, with details provided by Austin Stanley and Easton Freeze of AtoZ Sports, as well as Aaron Wilson of KPRC2:

The Thursday, October 15 practice at the Titans facility was especially heated, particularly between Jordan Elliott and 2024 1st-round pick OT J.C. Latham. A fight between the two occurred on the practice field, but initially other teammates and coaches chalked it up to emotions boiling over, fairly commonplace when it comes to the NFL.

Elliott continued yelling at Latham and was sent off the field — ending his practice early. Irate on the sideline, the defensive tackle removed his pads, threw them on the ground, and was recorded by security cameras leaving the team facility. Fellow defensive tackle John Franklin-Myers followed Elliott to talk to him further, meeting him at his vehicle in the player parking area next to the facility.

It’s reported that Elliott had gone to his vehicle to retrieve a firearm, allegedly with the intention of returning to the facility with it. Little is known about what Elliot’s intentions were with the weapon, but it has been reported that Franklin-Myers managed to convince his teammate not to retrieve the weapon. It’s unclear if Elliott returned to the practice facility, or left following the incident.

No incident report was filed with Nashville police. A source told Wilson that Elliott was having intense personal issues off the field involving his family, but “obviously he brought it to work with him.” In addition, the source added that everyone in the locker room felt that Elliott’s reaction was overblown and “crazy.”

Elliott did not play in the Titans’ win over the Colts on Sunday. The team reviewed the incident from the Thursday practice, much of which was captured on facility cameras, and made the decision to release him on Tuesday.

It’s the second bizarre event involving a player to happen to the Titans in less than a week. Top cornerback Alontae Taylor was a healthy scratch against the Colts, with Robert Saleh offering a rather cryptic update on the player’s future with the organization.

“As it pertains to Alontae, we’ll discuss it as a staff and make a decision that’s best for the team moving forward,” Saleh said.

Taylor was the team’s biggest free agent acquisition this past summer, while Elliott followed Saleh from San Francisco as a player the coach specifically wanted to be a part of his defense. Only six weeks into the season one has been released, and the other is seemingly on the trading block.

Busy day yesterday, so catching up with the Indianapolis Colts, where interim general manager Ed Dodds made his first roster moves in his position with the franchise for the remainder of the 2026 campaign:

It’ll be interesting to see how Dodds leaves his fingerprints on the franchise the next few months compared to his longtime GM predecessor, Chris Ballard, who was relieved of his duties earlier this week.

The 28-year-year old Harman, who was originally a 2019 2nd round pick of the Kansas City Chiefs, is most known for being a deep threat for that franchise. However, he’s bounced a round a bit since then, having also played with the New York Jets, Green Bay Packers, and Buffalo Bills organizations.

At 5,’10”, 187 pounds, Hardman has 178 receptions for 2,302 receiving yards (12.9 ypc. avg.) and 16 touchdown receptions during 82 career games (28 starts).

He appeared in 2 games for the Bills last season, but didn’t record a catch. He has not appeared in 2026 with an NFL team, but will be looking to continue his professional football career with the Colts.

Meanwhile, after punter Colts Rigoberto Sanchez suffered a big hit late on a blocked punt during Sunday’s brutal home loss to the Tennessee Titans, and sustained a foot injury, Indianapolis is bringing in veteran punter Thomas Morstead for insurance, should Sanchez be unavailable for this weekend’s road game against the Minnesota Vikings.

The 40-year-old longtime punter has appeared in 272 career games, and was the rookie punter for the New Orleans Saints during their 2009 upset Super Bowl win against the Indianapolis Colts. He actually executed the surprise second-half onside kick, which talk about a bad memory and a blast from the past.

Morstead punted for the San Francisco 49ers last year in all 17 games, averaging 43.6 yards per punt on his 44 punts, including 22 pinned within the opponent’s 20-yard line.

item.title: NFLSU rookie check-in: Week 7 preview
item.description: Some LSU rookies are getting increased snaps.
item.content:encoded:
CB Mansoor Delane

Another week, another great performance from Delane, and he is becoming one of the top players in the Defensive Rookie of the Year race. Delane is having one of the best rookie seasons we have seen from a DB in recent times, and he has been a major reason why the Chiefs are undefeated.

In Week 7, the Chiefs face the 2025/26 Super Bowl-winning Seattle Seahawks, a team that hasn’t met expectations this season. Delane has a chance to get a turnover in this matchup.

Safety A.J. Haulcy

Against the Titans, Haulcy got injured but returned. His impact was again minimal, so I wanted to talk about the Colts situation. Indianapolis just fired its general manager, and it looks like the head coach will be next. This could either be incredible for Haulcy or horrible. Given how high he was selected, any new coach will likely prioritize Haulcy’s potential, but they may not waste time on that if they prefer someone else. It’s going to be very interesting to see what happens.

WR Zavion Thomas

After seeing a rise in snaps in Week 5, Zavion Thomas had an even better game in Week 6. He went 3-for-3 on catches, and his speed after the catch was impressive. This positive trajectory for Thomas is exactly what you want to see from a rookie, and the Bears will likely get him even more involved against the Patriots in Week 7.

TE Bauer Sharp

It happened! Bauer Sharp finally got the first reception of his career, and it went for over 20 yards. Hopefully, this means Sharp will stay involved.

WR Barion Brown

I spoke about last week that Barion Brown needed to do better as a returner, and although it wasn’t perfect, he did just that against the Giants. He also made a great contested catch that showed some of the versatility he can bring to the offense.

In this week’s international game, the Saints will be in Paris, and it would be a great time for Brown to get the first return touchdown of his NFL career.

LB Harold Perkins

Interestingly, Perkins wasn’t used much against the Bears, but he did recover a fumble. There were injuries to the linebacker group, so it’s finally time for Perkins to take over the starting role, which will be a massive test to see if he can be a long-term option for Atlanta.

QB Garrett Nussmeier

Did not play because Patrick Mahomes is healthy.

EDGE Jack Pyburn

Was inactive for the Chiefs.

item.title: Cat Scratch Reader Reacts Survey: Updating your win predictions
item.description: The Panthers are not who we expected. What are they going to do with their next twelve games?
item.content:encoded:
The first six weeks of the 2026 NFL season are in the books and the 3-2 Carolina Panthers look far better than we expected. No, you didn’t expect Bryce Young to be leading the NFL with 309.8 passing yards per game.

Five games is enough of a sample size to say that something is definitely different this season. I can’t say that Young will continue his current pace of production, but I am confident that the Panthers won’t be in the market for a new quarterback at the top of the 2027 NFL draft.

With that in mind, it is time to update your total win predictions for the 2026 season. As a reminder, here is their full 2026 schedule:

That last fact, including the New Orleans Saints and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, accounts for ten of their remaining twelve games. The only two teams for whom the Panthers are not one of the top five or six hardest teams on their schedule are the Atlanta Falcons and the Minnesota Vikings.

item.title: Saints Rookie Report: Week 7 preview vs. the Steelers
item.description: We finally may see the complete class
item.content:encoded:
After a nearly disastrous loss to the New York Giants, the New Orleans Saints are facing another must-win situation against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the game will be played overseas in Paris.

In that Week 6 game, the Saints’ rookies put on some nice performances, and Week 7 may be the breakout game for this class.

WR Jordyn Tyson

Finally, we can talk about Jordyn Tyson. Although his availability for Sunday’s game is up in the air, he did travel with the team, which means there’s a chance he plays. The Saints’ offense has had a number of issues this season, and although Tyson will not fix everything, he is a massive upgrade over Bryce Lance. The injuries have been demoralizing, to say the least, but Tyson is an extremely talented player who can be one of the best WRs in the NFL. Although I would expect a small sample size if he does play, we may finally see him on the field.

DT Christen Miller

Although this was another game where the Saints went with other DT options over Miller, he did get on the field and helped shut down New York’s running game. In Week 7, the Saints face a much better rushing attack led by Jaylen Warren, so they will have to rely on Miller a bit more.

TE Oscar Delp

Against the Giants, Delp had his best game so far. He made some really important blocks that significantly helped the run game and had two catches. It wasn’t an incredible performance by any means, but one that could lead to more snaps for Delp.

Delp is likely going to be in the same exact role for Week 7.

OG Jeremiah Wright

Here we go!

After Cesar Ruiz left the game with an injury, rookie Jeremiah Wright was thrown into the lineup, and suddenly the run game looked great. Could this be a coincidence? Maybe. But it was clear that lanes were being opened up that the running backs could easily take advantage of. He got pushed back and beat at times, any rookie would, but overall, it was exactly what you wanted to see in his first real game. Now with Ruiz’s health in question, and the fact Wright’s debut was positve, the Saints must start him in Week 7. Might as well see what you have with Wright in a full game.

WR Bryce Lance

This was an up-and-down game for Lance. He once again had some head-scratching moments, including a drop, but he also scored the first touchdown of his young career. With Tyson’s return, Lance may be demoted to a more blocking role, but that may be better for now, especially as he develops.

WR Barion Brown

I thought Barion Brown had the best game of his career as well. He had some really nice returns and made a nice contested catch that may have been an interception if he didn’t get to the ball. Brown will likely fall to WR5 on the depth chart, but just like Lance, that’s perfectly fine.

RB CJ Donaldson

Another up-and-down game, Donaldson had some really nice runs to begin the game and fought for some tough yards. He nearly scored the first touchdown of his career, but was called back after his knee was down short. His blocking was also good, which was needed against the blitzes. Then we get to the fumble. The Giants’ comeback started after Donaldson fumbled, and that put a stain on this performance. Not sure if Donaldson will see fewer snaps in Week 7, but it’s something to monitor.

OT Mason Murphy

Murphy did not come into this game like last week, but after Asim Richards clear struggles against the Giants, it may be time for New Orleans to try something new.

DB Lorenzo Styles Jr.

Styles Jr. was once again an impact player on special teams, which is exactly why the Saints drafted him.

item.title: Streaky play by Jayden Daniels keeps pressure on head coach Dan Quinn - Daily Slop
item.description: "I just gotta execute better in that situation, regardless…. So just be better. I have to be better, you know” ~ Jayden Daniels
item.content:encoded:
The Daily Slop – 21 October 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

NFL.com

Commanders WR Terry McLaurin out for rest of season with torn patellar tendon

[T]ests on Tuesday showed that he suffered a torn patellar tendon that will sideline him for the remainder of the 2026 season, Quinn told reporters.

McLaurin will need to undergo surgery that will shelve him for the rest of his eighth NFL year. Having already missed one game this season due to a hamstring injury, the 31-year-old has now been struck the most severe injury of his career. He missed seven games in 2025, but that was due to a host of injuries: quad, core muscle and groin issues. 

Now, Diggs will presumably be quarterback Jayden Daniels’ top target with Dyami Brown, rookie Antonio Williams and Treylon Burks being forced into larger roles.

McLaurin, a five-time 1,000-yard receiver, finished the season with 15 receptions for 230 yards and one touchdown.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Commanders Roundtable

How Commanders can adjust to loss of Terry McLaurin

 It’s next man up.

Tight end Chig Okonkwo is starting to develop a solid connection with quarterback Jayden Daniels. Against the 49ers, Okonkwo recorded seven receptions for 69 yards, both of which were team highs. Last week against the New York Giants, he caught four passes for 60 yards, just two yards shy of McLaurin’s team-high total. After a rough start to the season, the former Tennessee Titan is beginning to find his groove and could become an even bigger part of Washington’s passing attack.

Another player Daniels needs to continue feeding is wide receiver Stefon Diggs. He leads the team in receptions with 24 and ranks second in receiving yards with 214. In three of the five games Diggs has played, he has recorded the second-most receiving yards on the team. With McLaurin potentially sidelined for an extended period, Diggs could become Washington’s top option at wide receiver.

The Commanders also have an under-the-radar weapon in their arsenal is wide receiver Antonio Williams. He ranks second on the team in receptions with 18 and third in receiving yards with 205.

Williams made an immediate impact in Week 1 against the Philadelphia Eagles, leading the team with 64 receiving yards on just four catches. He also had an 87-yard touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts that was nullified because of an illegal shift penalty.

Against San Francisco, Williams finished third on the team in receiving with 50 yards.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

NFL.com

Bad news, good news for Commanders

It has not been a good start to the season for Washington. The Commanders have managed only one win in six games — although it did come against the defending Super Bowl champions — and just fell short in a blowout-turned-nailbiter to the 49ers to fall to 1-4-1.

Luckily, that’s not a death sentence in this year’s NFC East, especially if the defense can maintain the form it found in the second half after allowing the most points in the league over the first five games. No one in the division has won a game since Week 4, marking the first time in league history every team in a division has played consecutive weeks without a victory, per NFL Research. It’s a feat made more (un)impressive by the fact that the Commanders and Giants went head-to-head in Week 5, a game that ended in a tie after disastrous overtime mistakes by both squads.

So, the Commanders are simultaneously at the bottom of the NFC East and in OK shape. They have the same number of losses as the Cowboys (2-4) and Eagles (2-4) and are by no means an impossible distance behind the first-place Giants (3-2-1). Only blind optimists would bank on Washington rebounding for a wild-card spot at this point, but there’s a path to the playoffs through the division. The Commanders can rest and reset during their upcoming bye with that in mind.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Review: Jayden Daniels vs 49ers

Statistically, Daniels played well, completing 29 of his 40 passing attempts for 300 yards and two touchdowns. But throughout the night, Troy Aikman on commentary was constantly pointing out mistakes and Daniels made a few more questionable decisions in clutch situations. So how did Daniels actually play?

Truthfully, I felt Daniels could have played a lot better than he did. That’s not to say he was bad or the reason the team lost this game, far from it. But Daniels is capable of being an outstanding quarterback and he fell short of that standard a number of times on Monday night. I’ll break down some of those mistakes and missed opportunities, but it’s also important to state that he did play well in large parts of the game too. So I’m breaking this post into two sections, the good and the bad. Let’s start with the positives.

Positives

Entering the game, the Commanders had struggled to generate many explosive plays this season and the 49ers defense has been very good at preventing them from happening. So it was a pleasant surprise to see Daniels and the Commanders offense were able to hit a couple of explosive plays throughout the game. One way they hit a couple early was on bootleg rollout schemes.

I have plenty of questions about the pre-snap operation with this Commanders offense right now. The amount of false starts and illegal shift penalties is unacceptable, and there’s quite a few plays where players are running around coming out of the huddle and don’t know where they’re going, leading to rushed snaps late in the playclock.

However, when Daniels is able to get the offense lined up and get a clean look at the defense, one of the key features of this offense from David Blough is the trust it gives to the quarterback to make checks at the line of scrimmage. We’ve seen both Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota make a bunch of checks at the line to get out of bad plays and into better ones. This game was no different, and Daniels made some critical checks in some big moments.

In the second half, and particularly late in the third quarter, Daniels really started to find a groove. He still had some errors, which we’ll get to, but he was much more consistent as the game progressed. He drove the team down the field on an 11-play touchdown drive that was capped off with a nice touchdown pass to Diggs.

The Athletic (paywall)

Against 49ers, Jayden Daniels again shows streaks of brilliance & lapses of concentration

That Washington fell to the 49ers on the road in primetime was not a surprise. Few, if any, expected a team with only one win, countless injuries and the most confounding mistake of the NFL season to have a real shot against one of the league’s most efficient teams.

That Washington turned it into a tight 23-17 finish and nearly had a chance to win after an abysmal first half was a reminder of Daniels’ rare ability — and the Commanders’ continued inability to give him help.

Two years ago, Daniels’ late-game, odds-defying heroics were enough. They were the hallmarks of his rookie season and they masked many of Washington’s struggles — on offense and defense.

Since then, as Daniels has struggled to stay healthy and as Washington has failed to find an identity, the Commanders’ shortcomings have been exposed repeatedly.

The Commanders have yet to play a clean game, free of self-inflicted and costly mistakes, like pre-snap penalties.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Heavy.com

Commanders’ Dan Quinn sends blunt message to Jayden Daniels

Dan Quinn knows the success of the Washington Commanders, not to mention his future as their head coach, largely depends on Jayden Daniels’ development in a new offense, but the under-fire boss isn’t above sending a blunt message to the star quarterback about how he needs to be better.

Quinn told ESPN’s John Keim on Tuesday, October 20, how, “like most things like with him there’s some plays that you say, ‘[Expletive], that’s an incredible throw,’ and there’s other ones I’d love him to stay through the look.”

Daniels is still trying to master an under-center offense under rookie coordinator David Blough. There were some obvious growing pains, but also plenty of positive signs, during the 23-17 defeat to the San Francisco 49ers on Monday Night Football.

Quinn “was hoping to see more of” Daniels playing “a more scramble-to-throw game” against the Niners’ zone coverage. The coach expects to see Daniels move the pocket with his legs and throw on the run more often “as he’s growing into it, more reps with David, more into the system, I’m expecting his out-of-pocket plays to continue, like for him to run keepers, you know, off our play-action game.”

That’s not exactly a glowing review of Daniels’ performance.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Sports Illustrated

At 1-4-1, Dan Quinn Says Trial and Error Is Over for Washington’s Offense

The Washington Commanders entered their bye week at 1-4-1, with more questions than answers as they look back on how they got here. This team started the season hell-bent on moving away from Jayden Daniels having to play hero ball. Now the team can only function correctly if he does. In the first half against the 49ers, the offense put up 90 yards and two first downs, then Daniels came out in the second and finished with 300 passing yards, two touchdowns, and only four rushes for 10 yards. Hard to imagine, but both versions of the offense showed up in one game.

Quinn wants a smaller set of things the team can execute repeatedly. He praised the offense for protecting the ball but said he wants more explosive plays. “Sometimes that can mean streamlining to say these are the eight things, 10 things that we’re going to over and over hit. … As the first part of the season goes, there’s some trial and some error, but now that we’re this far along, no more trial. This is how we want to get down.” I took Quinn’s ‘eight or 10 things’ comment as a plan to narrow what Washington leans on after the bye, rather than a promise to run only eight or 10 plays the rest of the season.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Washington Post (paywall)

The Commanders’ defense reached its potential for a half; that’s not enough

The struggling unit showed improvement in a 23-17 loss to the 49ers, but there’s still work to be done

[I]n the second half, defensive coordinator Daronte Jones’s unit did an about-face. It held the 49ers to just 67 yards after halftime and forced three consecutive three-and-outs to end the game.

“We just came out and played ball. It was nothing else. We was tired of getting hit in the mouth,” defensive tackle Tim Settle Jr. said. “We bowed up, and we played football in the second half.”

The Commanders had the benefit of getting cornerback Trey Amos and safety Nick Cross back from injury. Amos hadn’t played all season because of an ankle injury, while Cross had missed three games with an undisclosed internal injury.

Jones has been one of the most aggressive defensive play callers in the league, blitzing often in an effort to get the pass rush going, but it hasn’t paid enough dividends. At some point, the Commanders just need their players to perform better.

That finally started to click in the second half. Purdy lost wide receiver Mike Evans to an Achilles injury in the second quarter, which contributed to the drop-off. Washington also sacked Purdy twice and pressured him far more often.

The Commanders’ pass defense is the main reason they’re allowing 28.7 points per game (29th in the NFL). As long as that persists, the defense will keep weighing the team down.

Washington showed it can shut down an opponent in the second half against the 49ers. The next step is doing it for an entire game.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Commanders Roundtable

Studs & Duds in Washington’s loss to San Francisco

Stud

2nd Half Defense

Washington gave up three points in the second half on Monday night. Enter week six; their defense allowed 95 points in the second half. Washington forced three-and-outs on San Francisco’s final three drives to give them a chance to steal the upset.

Dud

1st Half Defense

San Francisco went down the field easily on the first two drives, with wide-open catches for Evans and tight end George Kittle. They were going to score a third touchdown, but linebacker Frankie Luvu recovered a fumble on McCaffrey near the field-goal line.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Commanders.com

5 takeaways from Commanders vs. 49ers

Jayden Daniels was impressive in the second half.

As frustrating as things were to start the night, the Commanders found a rhythm to close things out, and as mentioned above, it was nearly enough to overcome their self-inflicted mistakes.

Daniels finished the game with 300 yards and two scores and a completion rate of 72.5%. He’s 64.7% so far this season and has yet to commit a turnover. He’s 12th among quarterbacks in QBR and has seven total touchdowns. Although he is not perfect, he is playing well, and as he showed in the second half, that gives the Commanders a chance to beat anyone.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

A to Z Sports

Quinn shuts down any discussion of in-game confusion about down & distance

Far different from the mea culpa following the Giants debacle, DQ was unequivocal about his decision-making on 4th down vs the Niners

Quinn was asked after the game about the sideline reaction that had drawn so much attention during Washington’s loss.

His response was direct: He said he knew it was fourth down and that the Commanders had deliberately chosen to go for it.

According to Quinn, the conversation captured by the cameras concerned the illegal-shift penalty and a question over the headset about whether Washington could still attempt a field goal.

Quinn also explained that he expected a higher-scoring game against San Francisco and entered the matchup prepared to make aggressive fourth-down decisions.

That account offers a different explanation for the sideline reaction than the one circulating online. It does not erase the failed play, but it challenges the assumption that Quinn had simply forgotten the down.

Quinn’s explanation holds together. The illegal shift created confusion about whether a field goal was still on the table, someone asked him about it on the headset, & he answered. That’s a coach handling a procedural question in real time, not a coach who lost track of the down.

Quinn’s explanation is plausible and consistent with his stated plan to be aggressive.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Metro Sports Page

Sixpack of the Mondays: Gold Pants, Silver Linings

I was trying to think about past regular season games that I would have loved to get for two Sixpacks–that is to say, loved more than getting a warm 12-pack of that terrible Giants tie. Any of the wins during the seven-game winning streak in 2012 would have been great, including a 17-16 win over the New York Giants. That win took us to 6-6 on the season, hardly anything that would spark a parade, but it came on the heels of two straight wins against Philadelphia and Dallas.

There was something happening, and the league was officially on notice–hard to imagine after a horrific 3-6 start to the season. It was a nine-week stretch that bottomed out when Mike Shanahan stood at the podium after our sixth loss to the Carolina Panthers and announced that we were in “evaluation mode” in a way that very much sounded like we were sending the white flag to the top of the pole. But the Redskins came out in week 11 after the bye and picked up three wins against–wait for it–an incredibly weak NFC East. We sent the Eagles and Cowboys to 3-7 and 5-6, respectively.

The win put us one game back of the 7-5 NFC East-leading Giants. We raced past New York down the stretch, like RG3 galloping up the sidelines for his signature touchdown sprint against the Vikings earlier that season. What an incredible season that was…really just a “lightning strikes once” kind of thing, right?

That season was so different from this one, right? Mike Shanahan was a well-respected veteran coach. His players liked playing for him and he had enjoyed success at multiple stops in the league. His hiring signified a measure of organizational stabilization, but the job was just so gargantuan that we fans ran out of patience much faster than a top-tier head coach deserved.

We had a 31-year-old offensive coordinator that plenty of people thought very highly of–a young Kyle Shanahan. Dan Quinn is under fire to be sure, but there is no reason to believe we will see Josh Harris morph into the kind of owner who would fire coaches in week five–at least not under current circumstances. Battling impulsive desires and staying at the table to keep grinding is a move, too. The silence from the owner’s suite over the last week has been deafening, and I love it. McCarthy immediately energized the Giants offense with a 19-yard pass to Devin Singletary. Actually, it was a swing pass into the right flat that Singletary turned into a 19-yard gain. That’s how energized the offense was. 

McCarthy’s second pass landed near Charlie Jones’ feet. His third sailed out of bounds. His fourth was a pinpoint delivery to Martin Emerson. Emerson is a Saints cornerback, but admit it: you have trouble keeping track of the receivers on the Giants bench too, don’t you? I mean, seriously: Charlie Jones? Didn’t he make Bugs Bunny cartoons?

Under normal circumstances, Emerson’s interception would have all but ended the game. But the Saints are perennial doormats. The Giants play nothing but perennial doormats these days, as if all of their quality opponents joined the B1G, leaving them with nothing but a schedule full of Titans and Cardinals. They aren’t scheduled to face an opponent that currently has more than two wins until the Jaguars in Week 11.

Some Saints rando named CJ Donaldson fumbled the ball straight back to the Giants. And McCarthy isn’t the type of fierce competitor who will let a second chance on his second team in his third NFL season slip away.

McCarthy took the reins of the Giants offense and immediately handed off twice for five yards. The two runs ticked over a minute off the clock. It was as if John Harbaugh had conceded the loss. But McCarthy would not allow the coach or his teammates to surrender. He overthrew Malachi Fields along the right sideline on third down, shrewdly drawing a pass interference penalty.

Then McCarthy threw a 27-yard pass to a leaping Malik Nabers. It was a dime. It was a dart. Why do all lazy metaphors for passes sound like references to other Giants quarterbacks? One short completion and one near-interception by Emerson on a throw into double coverage in the end zone later, Tyrone Tracy ran for a touchdown. Game on, baby.

The Saints had a chance to run out the clock. But every team that faces the 2026 Giants immediately develops the time-management skills of habitual pot smokers. Tyler Shough threw a pair of incompletions in a three-and-out.

McCarthy went straight to work, launching an undercooked Chipotle burrito in the general direction of Jones. Defender Justin Reid helpfully deflected the pass into Jones’ hands. McCarthy then threw a sinkerball along the left sideline to a diving Emerson, who still plays for the Saints. Emerson appeared to intercept the pass, but he trapped the ball against the turf. 

Undaunted, McCarthy threw a touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely. It was a cutlet. A crab leg. 

McCarthy launched a 46-yarder to Nabers on the next series, after the Saints tried to find ways to add time to the clock. That pass set up a field goal. The Saints punted the ball back to the Giants with 14 seconds left on the play clock and the Giants out of timeouts after the two minute warning; if Kellen Moore tried to roast a turkey, he would die of salmonella. McCarthy scrambled up the middle for a long gain and threw completions in bounds, but he somehow ran out of time to lead a comeback.

The stat sheet says that McCarthy went 11-of-21 for 243 yards, one touchdown and one hand-wavable boo-boo. It doesn’t matter what the film or anyone else says.

Yes, McCarthy stunk in his first two NFL seasons. You know who else stunk in his first two seasons? Josh Allen. Have you heard of him? Are you vaguely aware of his backstory? Do you know what happened in his third season? No, I’m not gonna type it out. YOU say it. That’s right. He became awesome and stayed awesome. 

McCarthy has the potential to be even awesomer than Allen, because he was even worse than Allen in 2025. And in April through August, when he lost a Vikings quarterback competition to Kyler Murray, who plays football like a labradoodle puppy who doesn’t want to let go of a tennis ball. 

Harbaugh is rebuilding the Giants culture. And the best way to do that is to send a clear message to the locker room. Guys, I will bench any of you in a heartbeat for a one-hit wonder we brought in three weeks ago who got lucky on some turnover-worthy throws if it helps us achieve the short-term goal of stumbling into the playoffs Carolina Panthers-style. That’s how you build trust and camaraderie.

Assuming McCarthy doesn’t throw seven interceptions and get sacked nine times by the Texans in Week 7, he should have no trouble recreating the 9-7-1 glory of the 2022 Giants, the greatest Giants team anyone can remember. Then, Whammo! Dart will return in 2027. And then, Whammo! Dart will try to headbutt a truck, and guess who will be there to pick up the slack? That’s right: J.J. McCarthy. Unless the Colts sign him for four years at $160 million.

Loser: The Rams’ Special Teams (Forever and Always)

Somehow, amid all the fuck-them-picks, let’s-build-a-superteam bargaining the Rams have done with the football gods during Sean McVay’s decade in L.A., they wound up with the league’s most cursed special teams unit. That can be the only explanation at this point, right? We’ll let you have Matthew Stafford, but you’ll never have a reliable kicker, the gods must have said. Aaron Donald will come out of retirement, but every punt return will be an adventure.

The Rams’ special teams unit is a week-to-week punch line. Just a complete comedy of errors at this point. Six days after losing to the Bills on Monday Night Football because of a blocked field goal (that probably would have sailed wide anyway), and five days after cutting the Thicker Kicker (Harrison Mevis) and signing a svelte kicker (Blake Grupe), the Rams lost that new kicker to an injury when he tried to make a tackle on a kickoff return. The Rams then lost the game to the Cardinals 18-16. It’s ironic, probably, that the Cardinals won the game without scoring a touchdown; they just needed six field goals from their stalwart kicker, Chad Ryland.

Playing most of the game without a kicker meant that punter Ethan Evans had to handle kickoffs and that the Rams offense needed to go for two after their first touchdown (and they failed, hilariously so). When the Rams later had Evans attempt a PAT in the fourth quarter, backup QB Stetson Bennett had to enter the game as the new holder, and everyone at SoFi Stadium was probably holding their breath—even as the ball slipped between the uprights. 

The Rams rank last in total special teams EPA through Week 6—there’s such a massive gap between the Rams at no. 32 and the 49ers at no. 29 that even if San Francisco melts down on every kick return and field goal attempt on Monday night, it’s unlikely they’ll catch up to the Rams when it comes to special teams ineptitude. 

Special teams has been the Achilles’ heel of just about every McVay team. The Rams are last in special teams EPA since 2020 and have finished 30th or lower four times since then. They are well on their way to being not just last in the league in 2026 but one of the worst special teams units since 2000. They are averaging about six EPA lost on all special teams plays (kickoff and punt returns, field goal attempts, extra points, and two-point conversions). Of the 862 team seasons in the TruMedia database, the 2026 Rams rank 799th in special teams EPA. And if they continue at their current rate, they’ll become one of only two teams this quarter century to lose more than 100 EPA on special teams. (The 2000 Bills are last, with minus-109.45!)

And it’s not like this isn’t an acknowledged problem! This offseason, the Rams invested heavily in trying to fix what was the league’s second-worst special teams unit in 2025. McVay fired his ST coordinator before last season was even over and brought in Bubba Ventrone, a widely respected special teams coach who excelled as a ’teamer when he played in New England and as a young coach in Cleveland. The team signed a veteran long snapper, Joe Cardona, and linebacker Grant Stuard, a special teams coverage ace from Detroit. And yet the Rams continue to find new and increasingly embarrassing ways to lose games on special teams. They’ve now lost because of a kicker and because they’ve been without one. What fresh hell will the football gods inflict on the Rams next week?

item.description: Seattle continues their slide down the national power rankings
item.content:encoded:
Entering Week 6, the Seattle Seahawks slid back down the power rankings after losing to the San Francisco 49ers. After losing their second game in a row to the Denver Broncos, how much farther will they fall? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle.

Let’s start with the worst news. NFL.com dropped the Seahawks down three spots to 10th best in the NFL. In their ranking, they mention Sam Darnold’s “turnover problem.” However, they also remain optimistic that the offense as a whole can turn it around with the offensive line returning to full strength soon. B/R also dropped Seattle down three spots, from 6th to 9th. B/R also remains optimistic about the team considering their running back room is returning to health. However, they also mention the turnover issues as a big issue the team needs to address moving forward. 

Both CBS and PFT have the Seahawks ranked as 7th best in the league. PFT who moved the team down two spots simply state “[t]hey should’ve kept Kenneth Walker III.” CBS meanwhile didn’t move Seattle at all, and kept them ranked at number 7. In their ranking, CBS also highlighted that “Sam Darnold is turning the ball over way too much.” 

The highest ranking the Seahawks got from a national site this week was from ESPN, who ranked Seattle as the 6th best team in the NFL. Despite this higher ranking, ESPN also talked about the turnover issues. ESPN notes that the Seahawks have committed 12 turnovers, third most of any offense so far. Ten of those turnovers came in Seattle’s three losses. 

Overall, it would be surprising if the Seahawks did not drop down in the national power rankings. Losing two games in a span of five days will do that. Turnovers were the clear trend in all of these rankings. However, despite these woes the Seahawks are still firmly in the top ten of the NFL. 

Entering Week 6, the average power ranking between the five polled sites was 5.0. Entering week 7, that average has fallen to 7.8. The Seahawks face Kenneth Walker III and the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs next week on Sunday Night Football. Will Seattle be able to bounce back or will the slide down continue into week 8.

item.title: Bears-Falcons Upon Further Review – A Closer Look at the Referees
item.description: Our guy @GOOCH1701 takes a closer look at the referees in the Bears vs Falcons game.
item.content:encoded:
Hello Chicago Bears fans! Well, we are going to get into the calls this week in the Bears and Falcons game, but before that, let’s talk briefly about just how bad football officiating has been in 2026. First, on Saturday night, Florida State was robbed of an upset on a phantom holding call on their Hail Mary pass to the end zone. And then Notre Dame lost to BYU after their defense had an uncalled snap simulation infraction that led directly to a turnover with goal to go (not to mention I do not believe that the recovery was at all immediate). This was topped off by the referees screwing up the final play of the game, first ignoring an absolute mauling of the wide reciever in the endzone, and then finally calling the game when it was clear from both the booth and on-field clocks that there was still one second to go.

We hadn’t even gotten to the Sunday NFL games and the refs were getting bodied on X. The Big 12 admitted the officiating error after the game.

Anyway, let’s get back to the NFL and the Bears game. It. Did. Not. Get. Better. The Bears dominated most of the game against the Atlanta Falcons with Caleb Williams back in his first game since he injured his hamstring against the Vikings. This despite an extremely lopsided job of officiating by Scott Novak’s crew. Official totals: Chicago 12–133, Atlanta 4–31. That is the highest penalty yardage for the Bears in a decade. Jahdae Walker was ejected for a headbutt. The accepted tape is almost entirely on Chicago. This week the Bears Tax featured bad calls against the Bears and, perhaps more significantly, no-calls that were not made against the Falcons.

Same scale and weights. Upon Further Review grades every accepted flag and every tracked no-call in a Bears game (and the most controversial league-wide calls) using film, the rulebook, and a fixed scale.

Grading scale

  • Correct — Rule and tape agree.
  • Arguable — Judgment call; both sides are defensible.
  • Incorrect — Tape shows the crew got it wrong.
  • Horrible — Bright-line foul (or non-foul) a wing official should not miss.

Impact weight (1–4)

  • 1 — Housekeeping (false start, delay that doesn’t kill a scoring chance).
  • 2 — Drive disruption (down-and-distance flip, stalled series).
  • 3 — Scoring situation / red zone / automatic first that feeds points.
  • 4 — Wiped score or takeaway, dead drive flipped into points, or last-snap foul that would have been 1st-and-goal.

What gets reviewed

Replay reversals are graded against the clear-and-obvious standard for overturning the call on the field.

Every accepted flag against Chicago and against the opponent.

Key no-calls (especially those that create a “Bears Tax” pattern: unthrown flags on the opponent that mirror ones thrown on Chicago).

Accepted flags (Chicago-heavy)

The public box score and the postgame accounts are consistent on the big ones against Chicago:

  • Multiple offensive holdings (Benedet, Wright, Trapilo, others) that wiped chunk plays, including a 24-yard Odunze catch on third-and-7. The call against Wright on his pancake block was especially irksome.
  • Colston Loveland offensive pass interference that killed a would-be fourth-down conversion (this will feature in our Flag of the Game section). Horrible.
  • Jahdae Walker running into the punter in the third quarter after a third-down stop, giving Atlanta a first down at the CHI 35 instead of a punt. Correct. Wt 3.
  • Jahdae Walker’s unnecessary roughness/headbutt on Chris Blair on the kickoff after the Santos field goal that made it 31–7. Fifteen yards and an ejection. Correct. Wt 1 (already up 24).
  • False starts, delay of game, and the usual pre-snap clutter that pushed the total to 133 yards.

Against Atlanta the accepted flags are thinner: a Drake London roughing the passer, a Bijan Robinson holding that wiped a first down on a Gordon blitz, and a couple of others that total 31 yards. Novak’s crew was willing to throw on the Falcons when the hands were obvious. They were more willing to throw on Chicago.

No-calls against Atlanta (the Tax column)

This is the part the accepted totals do not show. When one side is flagged 12 times and the other four, the first question is whether the crew is seeing the same football game. The answer on the tape, from the all-22, is that Atlanta’s interior and edge were getting away with wraps that Chicago’s line was getting flagged for.

Interior holding on Williams’ dropbacks. Multiple snaps where an Atlanta lineman or tight end is grabbing a Bears rusher by the shoulder or jersey after the rush has already beaten the hands. Same wrap that produced Benedet and Wright holds on the other side of the ball. No flag. Incorrect no-call. Wt 2 on standard downs; Wt 3 on the ones that become sacks or pressures that force the incomplete. Williams was still sacked four times. Some of those were earned. Some of them were holds that stayed in the pocket.

Edge holding on the Gordon blitzes. The one that got thrown (Bijan on Gordon) shows the standard. There were others in the same family — hands outside the frame, body blocking after the whistle window — that did not. Arguable to Incorrect. Wt 2.

Pass interference / illegal contact on the Chicago receivers. Odunze and Burden were getting contacted early on intermediate routes without the flag. London’s RTP is the one that went the other way. The secondary contact was not balanced. Arguable no-call. Wt 2.

None of these is a Weight 4. Chicago still won by eight and led by 24. The Tax on Sunday didn’t cost the Bears the game, obviously. But the Tax was imposed nonetheless. Novak’s crew threw 12 flags on the visitors and four on the home team in a game where the home team’s line was not that clean at all from film-review. The very pattern this series of articles was designed to track.

First Quarter

CHI 0, ATL 0

Theo Benedet (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 12:07. 2nd-and-9 at the ATL 40. Sets up 2nd-and-19. Arguable. Wt 2.

Caleb Williams (CHI), delay of game, 5 yards — 8:47. 2nd-and-8 at the ATL 9 on the scoring drive. Process. Correct. Wt 1. Loveland’s 14-yard touchdown still stands. 7–0.

Swift scores from 4 yards later in the quarter. 14–0.

Second Quarter

CHI 14, ATL 0

Darnell Wright (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — ~9:16. After a Kalif Raymond catch. Enforced from the ATL 36. This is the pancake. Wright finishes the block, drives the defender to the ground with clean hands and body position, and the flag comes. A legal pancake is not a hold. The rule requires a grab, a tug, or a restriction that prevents the defender from pursuing. Wright’s hands were a bit outside, but this is a clean block. And finishing a block is football. Novak’s crew called the finish a foul. Horrible. Wt 2.

Additional holds in the same family pad the yardage. Arguable on the ones that are actual wraps. Wt 2.

LaCale London (ATL), roughing the passer, 15 yards — On an incomplete. Automatic first and yards for Chicago. Correct. Wt 3.

Third Quarter

CHI 21, ATL 7

Jahdae Walker (CHI), running into the kicker, 5/15 yards — Early third. After a third-down stop. Gives Atlanta a first down at the CHI 35 instead of a punt. Obvious. Correct. Wt 3.

Colston Loveland (CHI), offensive pass interference, 10 yards — ~7:31. 4th-and-2 at the ATL 41. Williams completes to Loveland for 10 yards to the ATL 31. First down. Flag. Enforced at the previous spot: 4th-and-12. Taylor punts. Atlanta starts at its own 6.

The contact is incidental or defender-initiated. A completed short conversion on fourth down is not offensive pass interference. The flag is late and unsupported. Horrible. Wt 3. What was a live first down in Falcons territory becomes a punt and a field-position gift. We will cover this one in the Flag of the Game feature.

Ozzy Trapilo (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — Negates a 24-yard Odunze catch on third-and-7. Arguable. Wt 3.

Roschon Johnson scores. 28–7.

Fourth Quarter

Santos from 50 makes it 31–7.

Jahdae Walker (CHI), unnecessary roughness (headbutt), 15 yards + ejection — On the kickoff after the field goal. Headbutt on Chris Blair after words. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

Atlanta scores twice in the final quarter (Pitts touchdowns, both two-point conversions good) to make the final 31–23.

Snapshot

Against Chicago: 12 accepted. Mostly Correct on the pre-snap and the Walker personal fouls. A handful of Arguable holds. The running-into-the-punter is Correct and costly. Walker’s ejection is Correct and ugly. The holding on Wright and the OPI on Loveland were Horrible.

Against Atlanta: 4 accepted. London RTP Correct. Bijan holding Correct. The rest process or gray.

No-call column against Atlanta: At least two Incorrect (interior holds) and two Arguable (edge and secondary contact). Not game-deciding. Still the imbalance.

Crew card (accepted): Mostly correct on Chicago’s self-inflicted laundry, but very light on Atlanta. Combined with the no-calls: Novak’s crew saw the visitors more clearly than the home team. Grade: Tax present, not decisive. Williams and the run game were better than the flags.

Against Chicago

Against Atlanta

Flag of the Game: Colston Loveland, Offensive Pass Interference
Q3, ~7:31. CHI 21, ATL 7. 4th-and-2 at the ATL 41.
Grade: Horrible. Weight: 3.

Chicago is in control. Caleb Williams is in his return game, the Bears have already scored three touchdowns, and they face fourth-and-2 from the Atlanta 41. The call is a short pass to Colston Loveland on the left. He catches it and is marked at the ATL 31 for a 10-yard gain and a first down. The completion is the play until the flag arrives.

Scott Novak’s crew throws offensive pass interference on Loveland. Enforced at the previous spot: 4th-and-12 at the CHI 49. Tory Taylor punts. Atlanta starts the next drive at its own 6. A live fourth-down conversion in Falcons territory becomes a punt and a field-position gift.

The rule is not subtle. A receiver may not initiate contact that significantly hinders a defender’s ability to play the ball. Legal positioning and incidental contact are not fouls. The available angles show the defender initiating or the contact remaining incidental to a contested short catch. Kevin Fishbain called it “pretty ticky tack” in real time. Other views from the afternoon noted the defender as the initiator and the flag as late—thrown after the catch was already the story. This is not a gray push-off that required some kind of a judgment call. It is throwing yellow laundry on a great play by the tight end – the crew invented a foul that the tape does not support.

Horrible is the grade when a wing official throws a flag the rule does not allow, or fails to throw one the rule requires. Here the contact does not meet the standard for offensive pass interference. The flag should have stayed in the pocket. Instead, it wiped a first down, forced a punt, and handed Atlanta the ball at its own 6 while Chicago was already being flagged at a decade-high rate.

The weight is 3 because it kills a conversion in plus territory. The game state keeps it from being a 4—the Bears still led 21–7 and won 31–23—but the call itself is a bright-line miss. Loveland finished with six catches for 65 yards and a touchdown. This is the one that did not count, and the one that should have.

League file — Flags of the Week
Two roughing-the-passer calls, Cowboys at Packers
Sunday Night, Oct. 18. Lambeau Field. Packers 23, Cowboys 13.
Crew: Craig Wrolstad.

I hate to say anything about the Packers getting screwed by the officials, because so often it is the other way around. But in a weekend with absolutely egregious calls all over the league, both in terms of significance and frequency, these two phantom RTPs really stood out. Green Bay led 23–7 in the fourth quarter when the flags arrived. Both were on Packers defenders against Dak Prescott. Both kept a Dallas drive alive. Neither produced points. Both, though, became part of the national conversation on the horrible, terrible, really no-good officiating of the NFL this season.

Flag 1: Lukas Van Ness, roughing the passer, 15 yards.
~7:44 remaining, fourth quarter. GB 23, DAL 7.
Grade: Incorrect. Weight: 4.

Prescott looks for Jonathan Mingo. Carrington Valentine steps in front and intercepts. It is Green Bay’s third takeaway of the night. The flag is already out. Van Ness is called for roughing. The pick comes off the board. Dallas keeps the ball, gains 15 yards, and the drive continues.

The tape shows a two-handed push after the ball is gone. It is slightly late, but there isn’t even a single step made by Van Ness before the contact. It is not high. It is not driven with force. Prescott goes to the ground, but the contact is a shove rather than a hit that lands with body weight or targets the head/neck. The rule protects the quarterback from unnecessary or excessively late contact once the ball is released. It does not turn every post-release touch into a 15-yard foul. This one is an egregious soft call where the force does not match anything close to a justified flag. Brett Kollmann called it “the most un-American roughing the passer call in history.” Charles Woodson posted that the league has to do something about these calls. Lambeau booed their hearts out. Van Ness put his hands on his head out of disbelief. The interception that should have ended the drive did not.

Dallas failed to cash it. The drive eventually stalled on downs after a later sack by Van Ness and a fourth-and-11 throw out the back of the end zone. The Weight is still 4 because a takeaway was wiped. A dead drive became a live one. That is the definition of the highest impact grade even when the points do not follow.

Flag 2: Karl Brooks, roughing the passer, 15 yards.
Same drive, later in the fourth.
Grade: Incorrect. Weight: 3.

Lambeau got the boo-birds out again. Brooks is flagged for contact that hits Prescott around the middle and drives him down. The description from the postgame accounts is a body shot after the release, not a helmet shot and not a lift-and-slam. It is another automatic first and another 15 yards on a drive that already survived one wiped interception. The crew treated it, I believe, as a “full weight” tackle, but the replay clearly shows Brooks coming down on the side of Prescott – not on top of him. The available angles do not show the force or the timing that turns a standard rush into roughing. It is the second soft RTP on the same series.

There was a third roughing call on the night (Evan Williams, contact near the helmet area on a block attempt) which was also iffy, and the Packers finished with three RTP flags total, raising their season total to a league-leading six. Matt LaFleur’s postgame line was measured: he wants the rule called both ways, and he noted Jordan Love has absorbed 39 hits without drawing one. The national tape, though, settled on the two that kept the Dallas drive alive.

Why these are the Flags of the Week

The competition was stiff this week. Beyond the two soft roughing-the-passer flags that wiped a Packers interception and extended a Dallas drive on Sunday night, Week 6 produced several other calls that drew immediate pushback. In London, Shawn Hochuli’s crew negated a Bhayshul Tuten touchdown with an offensive holding penalty on Brenton Strange that multiple angles and NFL insider Jordan Schultz showed as nothing more than incidental contact or a slip—no jersey grab—costing Jacksonville six points and contributing to a season in which the Jaguars have already had five touchdowns erased by flags. Later in the same game, Travis Hunter was called for defensive pass interference in the end zone on Nico Collins with 20 seconds left in the half; Ryan Clark and others called it non-existent contact that set up a Houston score and flipped the lead. Hours earlier in Kansas City, Ashton Gillotte was flagged for roughing Justin Herbert on a play that wiped a Chris Roland-Wallace interception; rules analyst Gene Steratore said he “just didn’t like the foul,” noting Gillotte appeared to avoid full contact. The common thread was the same one visible in Green Bay: crews throwing or withholding flags in ways that altered scoring plays or takeaways without clear support on the tape.

For our two in the Packers-Cowboys game, the rule is supposed to protect quarterbacks from unnecessary force, late hits with body weight, and contact to the head or neck. It is not supposed to turn every post-release shove or midsection drive into an automatic first down and a wiped takeaway. On Sunday night, in front of a national audience, Craig Wrolstad’s crew threw two of them on the same drive – arguably three. One erased an interception. Both were soft enough that the reaction was immediate and nearly universal. Green Bay still won. Dallas still failed to score on the drive. That does not make these calls any less egregious.

Grade on the pair: both Incorrect. The Van Ness flag is Weight 4 because it killed a takeaway. The Brooks flag is Weight 3 because it extended a scoring opportunity that had already been gifted. Together they are the clearest example this week of a rule being enforced past the point the tape supports.

And finally – while you might be tempted to wonder if this is all just anecdotal and driven by social media, consider these stats that Warren Sharp and Kirsten Tanis reported this week:

But what did you think about the flags and no-calls in the Bears vs Falcons game? Was the Bear Tax in full effect? What do you think about the increase in controversial calls and flags in general around the NFL? Tell us in the comments below!

item.title: AP Chiefs Mailbag: When will Cyrus Allen see the field?
item.description: Arrowhead Pride staff writer Jared Sapp answers your questions about Kansas City after another divisional win.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag!Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs!

The Chiefs are 5-0 after a 22-6 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers that left many fans wondering why the team didn’t look more dominant in a divisional victory that never truly seemed in doubt. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds.

FoxBox2021 asks:


If wide receiver Rashee Rice stays out longer, and Xavier Worthy has more performances like he did against the Chargers, would it be likely the Chiefs would be comfortable in letting Rice walk in free agency?

I think Rice’s first taste of free agency after the season is going to be complicated. Beyond demonstrating that his off-field issues are behind him, Rice entered 2026 needing to prove that he can stay healthy. Other than six offensive snaps in Week 4, he has now missed two games.

Worthy has played well in the last two games. One thing that always frustrates me about the third-year pro is that he was drafted to provide a vertical element to complement what the Chiefs have in Rice. However, some of Worthy’s best games have come in essentially Rice’s catch-and-run role when the troubled wideout has missed. It was definitely encouraging to see Worthy reel in seven passes for 73 yards against the Chargers. However, he also finished the game with a 4.3-yard average depth of target (ADoT). That is not the player he was drafted to be.

Ultimately, I still expect Rice to somehow still be a Chief in 2027, even if it is on an incentive-laden “prove it” deal. Should a bidding war unexpectedly open for his services, however, the Chiefs should feel pretty confident they can get much of the production from Worthy, who will likely be entering his own contract season in 2027 unless the Chiefs exercise an expensive fifth-year option for 2028.

TheSovereign1587 asks:


It seems rookie pass rusher R Mason Thomas is beating blockers regularly, creating pressures but can’t seem to close the deal with sacks. From a coaching/technical standpoint, what does he need to do to take the next step and start getting sacks?

I am very confident that as Thomas gets more time in the film room with a veteran coaching staff, he will hone his craft. His first five games should provide some good experience to build on. Though Kirk Cousins and Justin Herbert take more than their share of sacks, both are crafty veterans who know how to get the ball off quickly to thwart a rookie pass-rushing technique. He also has film to study of going against a mobile quarterback in Malik Willis.

Sacks can sometimes come in bunches, and I won’t be surprised if there is a stretch where Thomas turns his high pressure rate into prettier results on the stat sheet.

Most rookie pass rushers take time getting acclimated. The player Thomas is most often compared to is Nik Bonitto of the Denver Broncos, who ended his rookie season with only 1.5 sacks and six pressures. Thomas already has more pressures through five games (nine) than a player considered with the league’s best had as a rookie.

BuckeyeChief asks:


Is what the Chiefs are doing sustainable for a deep playoff run and will they trade for help at WR before the Nov. 10 deadline?

I think Kansas City’s defense is playing well, but I think they will be playing even better as the playoffs near. I expect the young talent will be a more well-rounded unit than the famous 2022 squad that boasted multiple rookie starters.

I am not sure what the offense is doing through five games is sustainable. Perhaps Kenneth Walker really is just a Derrick Henry-level running back that is ready to hold up to extreme usage. However, I think the team has to find a way to involve rookie Emmett Johnson more in the run game. Johnson’s potential on screen passes is also one of the most feasible ways for Kansas City to raise the floor and ceiling of the offense.

In the receiving game, I think the Chiefs can win a lot of games with the current group, but the depth is already being tested. Not having Tyquan Thornton to take the top off of defenses is also an issue that now must be worked around. The floor of the current receiving room also depends on tight end Travis Kelce continuing a high snap count and remaining a top focus of opposing defenders.

A month from now, I do predict that there will be at least one wide receiver added. I am not sure if that will come via trade or a reunion with the ever-controversial Tyreek Hill. Unless the Chiefs find an opportunity to add a cost-controlled talent with high upside, I suspect the focus will be on adding a situational deep threat, rather than someone to replace any of the current starters.

da’Monk asks:


What dead money sits on kicker Harrison Butker’s contract and is there an upside, financially, to cutting him now?

There is no financial benefit to the Chiefs were they to release Butker during the season. They would still owe the remainder of his $5.8 million base salary for 2026. Because he cannot be replaced with an unpaid intern, the move would cost salary cap space as his hypothetical replacement’s salary is added.

I do not expect Butker to be released during the season. If his struggles become too much for the Chiefs to work through, my guess is you would see a mystery placement on Reserve/Injured.

NFL players truly enter contract seasons in the last year that their salary is guaranteed. Although Butker is nominally signed for two more seasons, I do not expect him to be brought back at his current non-guaranteed $5.7 million salary for 2027. The Chiefs will be able to save $4.4 million against the 2027 cap by moving on while leaving a $2.8 million deal money charge.

Otis#89 asks:


What needs to be done to fix the short yardage issues?

The Chiefs have not run a quarterback sneak since the night the world saw Patrick Mahomes’ kneecap put back into place on the field in Denver in 2019. Once again, opposing defenses knowing that Mahomes is not going to push forward for a first down seems to limit what the Chiefs can do.

We have seen Kansas City use tight ends for quarterback sneaks with Blake Bell and Noah Gray in the past. Every time that has been used, however, it seems to be something defenses solve very quickly.

One possible path would be to have quarterback Justin Fields situationally on the field for short yardage. I wonder if that is something we will see in the weeks to come.

With third-string running back Brashard Smith seeming to have no role on either offense or special teams, I have seen some thoughts of replacing him with veteran Kareem Hunt, who was unstoppable on short conversions in 2025. It would still seem difficult to use a roster spot on a running back who would only be used in one specific case.

The Chiefs have a very veteran offensive staff, and their offensive coordinator and running backs coach played a combined 241 games in NFL backfields. This is a clear weakness of the team that they have to find the solution to before it is too late.

Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! We will be back after the Chiefs to face the Seattle Seahawks on next week’s “Sunday Night Football.” Keep watchingThe Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.

item.title: Bills had a 2nd spitter in Las Vegas
item.description: NFL has suspended another Buffalo DB for spitting at Raiders’ players
item.content:encoded:
In a bizarre and disturbing twist, the NFL announced Wednesday morning that it has suspended another Buffalo Bills’ defensive back for spitting at a Las Vegas Raiders’ player in the Bills’ 33-30 victory.

The league suspended defensive back/special teamer Sam Franklin for spitting. He will serve a one-game suspension against the Baltimore Ravens when the Bills returner from their by after Week 7. Monday, the NFL suspended Buffalo defensive back C.J. Gardner-Johnson for spitting.

Gardner-Johnson eject before halftime for spitting in the direction of Raiders’ tight end Brock Bowers. Gardner-Johnson was also suspended for the Baltimore game.

Franklin’s incident occurred with 1:32 remaining in the game after a Raiders’ extra point on their final touchdown. Franklin is reportedly denying the act and will appeal the suspension. Video shows Franklin and Raiders’ tackle D.J. Glaze having a confrontation after the kick.

The NFL is cracking down on such incidents, but it is highly unusual for two players from the same team to get such suspensions.

item.title: Released Titans player nearly confronted teammate with gun: Reports
item.description: The Titans released Jordan Elliott after an incident in practice involving a gun and JC Latham, according to multiple reports.
item.content:encoded:
More details have emerged surrounding the Tennessee Titans' seemingly sudden decision to release defensive tackle Jordan Elliott.

According to Aaron Wilson of KRPC Houston and Austin Stanley and Easton Freeze of AtoZSports.com, Elliott went to his car to grab a gun after a heated dispute in practice with teammate and offensive tackle JC Latham on Thursday, Oct. 15.

Wilson reported that Elliott was told to leave the field after getting into it with Latham in practice. The defensive tackle reportedly removed his pads on the sideline, "stormed out" of the Titans' locker room and went to the players' parking lot to his car to retrieve a gun.

JORDAN ELLIOTT: Titans release veteran defender after 'incident' at team facility

Titans defensive tackle John Franklin-Myers stepped in to de-escalate the situation, according to reports. No one filed a report to the Metro Nashville Police Department, according to The Tennessean, part of the USA TODAY Network.

Elliott was ruled out of the Titans' Week 6 game against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday, Oct. 18, for personal reasons. Two days later, on Tuesday, Oct. 20, the Titans announced they were releasing Elliott.

"On Thursday, October 15, there was an incident at our team facility involving Jordan Elliott," the statement said. "Following our review of the incident, we have made the decision to release Elliott from our roster. We will have no further comment on the matter."

Titans head coach Robert Saleh is expected to hold his weekly press conference with reporters at 12:25 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Oct. 21.

THE TENNESSEAN: Former Titans player Jordan Elliott was released after gun incident, per reports

Prior to his release, Elliott was in the first year of a two-year, $8 million deal he signed with the Titans in March. He totaled 11 tackles in five games with one start.

Elliott began his career as a third-round pick by the Cleveland Browns in the 2020 NFL Draft. He signed a two-year contract with the San Francisco 49ers in free agency before the 2024 season. Across three teams and seven seasons in the NFL, Elliott has appeared in 102 games with 65 starts. He has tallied 159 tackles and five sacks in his career.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Released Titans player nearly confronted teammate with gun: Reports

item.title: Bengals Progress Report: Grading the Offense
item.description: Here’s the offense’s grade after the first five weeks of the season.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals are coming out of their bye week. They’re 3-2, and so far, it’s been a pretty mixed bag so far.

They started the season looking dominant against the Buccaneers and Texans (who have won just two games between them at this point in the season), but then suffered frustrating losses to the Steelers and Jaguars before escaping Miami with an ugly victory over the winless Dolphins in Week 5.

So, yeah. Mixed bag.

Since there’s no Bengals football to watch this weekend, let’s take a look at how the rushing and passing offenses have performed through the first five games, assign each a grade, and then determine an overall offensive grade.

Starting with…

Rushing Offense

Zac Taylor, once again, entered the season talking a big game about establishing a more balanced offense. The Bengals spent much of training camp working on Joe Burrow taking snaps under center, and they really tried to force the issue through the first few games of the season.

It hasn’t exactly worked.

The Bengals have the seventh-fewest rushing yards in the league, are averaging just 3.6 yards per carry, and have scored only two rushing touchdowns this season. Perhaps most damning of all, their longest run of the season is just 13 yards, the shortest of any team’s longest run in the NFL. And that run came all the way back in Week 1.

Chase Brown has significantly out-carried Samaje Perine so far, 71-27, but that trend shifted somewhat in Week 5 against the Dolphins. The Bengals appeared to abandon their commitment to running with Burrow under center and instead leaned more heavily on running out of shotgun, an approach that seems better suited to Perine.

Of course, Brown has also proven himself to be a reliable receiver out of the backfield, so he shouldn’t have much trouble staying on the field moving forward. Meanwhile, it’s become painfully obvious that the Bengals coaching staff has little, if any, confidence in Tahj Brooks.

For the first time in Burrow’s career, he has the same five starting offensive linemen in front of him for consecutive seasons. While they’ve done a better job protecting him than in years past, this offensive line was built primarily to keep Burrow upright, not necessarily to open up running lanes.

Ultimately, the running game has been a disappointment, but there is one important thing worth pointing out.

According to PFF, the four highest-graded run defenses in the NFL belong to the Buccaneers, Steelers, Jaguars, and Texans, with grades of 79.5, 76.3, 75.0, and 74.8, respectively.

In other words, four of the Bengals’ first five opponents have been among the league’s best at stopping the run.

Meanwhile, Cincinnati’s rushing offense ranks 18th in the NFL with a PFF grade of 70.9.

That’s worth considering before completely writing off the running game, but the production simply hasn’t been good enough.

Rushing-Offense Grade: 71% (C-)

Passing Offense

This is the identity of the Bengals’ offense, and it’s not particularly difficult to understand why.

Burrow is an elite quarterback, and Cincinnati boasts the best wide-receiver duo in the NFL in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, both of whom would be legitimate No. 1 receivers on just about any team in the league.

The offensive line was built to keep Burrow clean, and so far, it’s done an okay job. Considering what we’ve seen from Bengals offensive lines in recent years, that’s actually something of a compliment.

Chase and Higgins are weapons 1 and 1A. Opposing defenses understandably do everything they can to take them away, which creates opportunities for players like Mike Gesicki, Dohnte Meyers, and Brown coming out of the backfield.

Unfortunately, Andrei Iosivas landed on injured reserve after tearing a ligament in his thumb that required surgery. While he’s expected to return at some point this season, his absence has exposed a considerable gap between the Bengals’ top two receivers and the rest of the depth chart.

Through five games, Burrow has thrown for 1,361 yards (sixth in the NFL), 11 touchdowns (fourth), and just three interceptions (tied for the second-fewest). Higgins leads the team with 423 receiving yards, while Chase and Gesicki have each caught four touchdown passes.

Those are impressive numbers, especially considering the Bengals have struggled to establish any sort of consistent rushing attack. Opposing defenses know Cincinnati wants to throw the football, and Burrow and company have still managed to put up strong numbers through the air.

There have been some frustrating stretches, though, and the passing game hasn’t always looked as explosive or consistent as you’d expect from an offense featuring this much talent.

Still, if this is what a typical “slow” start looks like for Burrow and the Bengals’ passing offense, there’s reason to believe they could come out of the bye week firing on all cylinders.

Hopefully.

Passing-Offense Grade: 89% (B+)

The Bengals’ offense has as much star power as any unit in the NFL, but far too often, it seems to get in its own way.

Taylor’s play-calling can be frustratingly conservative, and at times, the offense lacks the creativity you’d expect from a unit with so many talented players demanding touches.

The inability to establish a consistent rushing attack has made the offense increasingly one-dimensional, placing even more pressure on Burrow and his receivers to carry the load.

Fortunately, they’re talented enough to do exactly that.

But there’s a difference between having the talent to be one of the NFL’s best offenses and actually performing like one week in and week out.

Through five games, the Bengals’ offense has been good. Not great, but good.

Overall Offensive Grade: 80% (B-)

item.title: Second Bills player suspended for spitting at Raiders player
item.description: Bills defender C.J. Gardner-Johnson apologized for spitting on Raiders star Brock Bowers. Now another Bills player has been suspended spitting in the same game.
item.content:encoded:
A Buffalo Bills defensive back has been suspended one game for spitting at an opponent during the team's win Sunday, Oct. 18, over the Las Vegas Raiders.

And it wasn't C.J. Gardner-Johnson.

Bills defensive back Sam Franklin Jr. will serve the one-game ban without pay "for an act of unsportsmanlike conduct," the NFL said in its announcement of the suspension.

According to the league's version of events, with 1 minute, 32 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter following Las Vegas’ successful extra point attempt, Franklin Jr. spit at an opponent. That violated Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to “any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship.”

Franklin Jr.’s suspension begins on Monday, Oct. 26. He will be eligible to return to the Bills’ active roster on Monday, Nov. 2, following the team’s Nov. 1 game against the Baltimore Ravens. Franklin Jr. spent the first five seasons of his career (2020-24) with the Carolina Panthers and joined the Bills last season.
