item.title: Patriots vs. Bears series history ahead of Week 7
item.description: The most memorable moments of the Patriots-Bears series, relived.
item.content:encoded:
Following a game against their division rival Jets, the New England Patriots are up against a relatively unfamiliar opponent. They will travel to Chicago this week to take on the Bears on Thursday Night Football. It will be only the 17th meeting between the two storied franchises.

Let’s take a look back at the most important moments from the first 16.

Patriots vs. Bears series history

Overall history: Even though the most memorable game of the series is a Bears win, it is the Patriots who have won the majority of the first 16 contests between the two organizations. New England holds an 11-5 edge after winning six of eight games since 2000. Those include a come-from-behind victory in 2002 that saw Tom Brady and company erase a 27-6 deficit in the late third quarter to ultimately win 33-30, as well as a lopsided 51-23 win during the 2014 season that was dominated by Rob Gronkowski and his three touchdowns. Chicago, as we will discuss shortly, is 1-0 against the Patriots in the playoffs.

First game: Three years after the AFL-NFL merger, the Patriots and Bears met for the first time. The game at Soldier Field was a defensive affair that saw the two teams combine for only 98 net passing yards as well as six turnovers. Five of those were forced by New England, putting the team on the path to success. The winning points were scored in the fourth quarter, when quarterback Jim Plunkett found the end zone on a 5-yard quarterback keeper to give the Patriots a 13-10 win. Neither they nor the Bears were overly successful as a whole in 1973, though. | Highlights

Most memorable game: Unfortunately for the Patriots, the most memorable out of their meetings with the Bears is Super Bowl XX. New England did manage to take a 3-0 lead and by doing so score the first points of the playoffs against Chicago’s famous 46 defense, but it ultimately was unable to hang on: the NFC champions scored 44 unanswered points, including the famous 1-yard rushing touchdown by defensive tackle William “Refrigerator” Perry in the third quarter. When all was said and done, the team of head coach Raymond Berry finished with just 123 net yards and turned the ball over six times en route to a 46-10 blowout that was the most lopsided defeat in a Super Bowl at the time. | Highlights

Most recent game: The Patriots’ most recent matchup with the Bears brought more pleasant memories than the 1986 defeat, albeit at a smaller scale. Meeting at Soldier Field in 2024, the team led by then-head coach Jerod Mayo and then-rookie quarterback Drake Maye celebrated a 19-3 win. Maye was solid, but the defense was the story of the day: led by Deatrich Wise Jr. and Anfernee Jennings, who each registered two takedowns, the Patriots sacked Caleb Williams nine times and limited Chicago to 142 yards. | Highlights

The Patriots and Bears will add to their series history on Thursday at 8:20 p.m. ET.

item.title: Jaguars Reacts Survey: Will Jacksonville win the AFC South this season?
item.description: Do you trust the Jaguars to protect their two-game lead in the division?
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Jaguars fans and fans across the country.

The Jacksonville Jaguars just can’t seem to get past the Houston Texans.

The Jags have a 13-3 record in their last 16 regular season games, but two of those three losses came against the Texans, including Sunday’s 31-34 stunner.

“That was not the result that you hunt up each week,” head coach Liam Coen said Monday.

“You never want to lose, but I am glad that we’re able to respond in terms of the mental toughness of the group when it’s not perfect or everything’s not going exactly according to plan, and they just keep playing their tails off.”

The Week 6 loss to Houston was a bummer, as was Jacksonville’s 10-point blown lead to Denver in Week 2. At the end of the day, though, the Jaguars have a 4-2 record going into their bye. They lead the AFC South by two games over the Texans (2-4), Indianapolis Colts (2-4), and Tennessee Titans (1-5). And it’s not fraudulent at all.

The top four teams in point differential this year are the Jaguars (+50) and the three remaining undefeated teams: the San Francisco 49ers (+67), Kansas City Chiefs (+57), and Minnesota Vikings (+45).

Jacksonville has performed like one of the best teams in the NFL — despite facing the league’s seventh-toughest schedule so far this season, per Sharp Football Analysis. They’re projected to have the single easiest schedule the rest of the way.

“To be six weeks in and to feel confident that your team’s going to respond, that we’re made of the right stuff to respond, and we have so much football left that you’re excited about,” Coen said.

“You’re excited about getting things corrected; you’re excited about being able to be in those moments again and maybe do it right or do it better the next time, as much as it hurts in the moment, in the aftermath. But I have a lot of confidence in this football team. Trevor [Lawrence] gives me so much confidence on a weekly basis as a play caller and the way that I think he’s seeing it right now and playing. I’m very excited about this football team.”

Did the latest loss to Houston make you worried about Jacksonville’s lead in the division? Or do you feel comfortable predicting them to win the AFC South for a second straight season?

item.title: Week 7 NFL Power Rankings: Does close scare drop 49ers this week?
item.description: Are the Niners still deserving of the top spot in the power rankings?
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers have been sitting atop the NFL’s power rankings for a few weeks now, as they remain just one of three unbeaten teams in the league.

That remained true after Week 6, as the 49ers escaped by the Washington Commanders 23-17 in a game that went down to the final plays as the defense made a stand. San Francisco really struggled to generate offense without Mike Evans, while Jayden Daniels threw for 300 yards against the 49ers defense, leading to a closer game.

Nonetheless, San Francisco is 6-0, becoming the lone team in the NFL to win six games thus far. Given how close the game was and how other teams fared this weekend, did the 49ers get docked in the power rankings this week?

Let’s look at several Week 7 power rankings to see the consensus.

ESPN: No. 1

The 49ers remained the top team here as they remain one of the teams without many actual flaws with their play. When highlighting the team’s biggest issue on offense so far, the answer was clear: receiver injuries.

“The Niners haven’t had many problems in terms of production, but they have had a significant amount of attrition at wideout,” ESPN’s Nick Wagoner wrote. Ricky Pearsall (knee), De’Zhaun Stribling (ankle), Christian Kirk (calf) and Demarcus Robinson (ankle) were supposed to be four of the team’s top five receivers and all landed on IR before Week 3.

“That doesn’t account for Deebo Samuel Sr.’s multiweek hamstring injury or the various bumps and bruises Mike Evans played through before departing Monday night’s game with Achilles tendinitis. The good news? Most of them are expected back this season, but the 49ers have had to scramble in the meantime.”

Behind the 49ers were the Kansas City Chiefs, who improved to 5-0 off a dominant win over the Los Angeles Chargers. Rounding out the top five were the Buffalo Bills, Minnesota Vikings, and the Jacksonville Jaguars.

NFL.com: No. 1

NFL.com’s Nick Shook did note that there could be some question to San Francisco’s standing atop the rankings after the win, but kept them at No. 1 still after six weeks over the Chiefs.

“San Francisco flirted with an epic collapse, but the same battered defensive line came through again in the final moments, sacking Jayden Daniels to bury Washington’s comeback bid,” Shook said. “The fashion in which this game ended might cause some to question the 49ers’ standing atop the Power Rankings; we often fail to remember, however, that there are professional football players on both sides (and the Commanders feature a dynamic quarterback in Daniels).

“Kyle Shanahan’s propensity for letting things get a little too close for comfort reared its unwelcome head again, but San Francisco finished the job like a proven winner usually does. Let’s not allow the anxiety-inducing fourth quarter to overshadow how dominant the Niners were earlier in the game. They’re undefeated and keeping the throne.”

Behind the 49ers were the Chiefs, Bills, Vikings, and Jaguars. Complete unity here with ESPN’s list with the exact same top five.

CBS Sports: No. 1

It was simple here for CBS’s Pete Prisco, as the 49ers found a way to win again.

“They made it interesting against the Commanders, but they still found a way,” Prisco wrote. “Now they face a long road trip to play the Falcons on a short week.”

There was a slightly different top five here, as the Chiefs, Vikings, Bills, and Denver Broncos followed. The Broncos offense has been a big story, but they’re 4-2 after facing one of the tougher schedules in the NFL to start the season.

FOX Sports: No. 1

The Niners remained at No. 1 here as well, with FOX Sports’s Ralph Vacciano lauding the team’s depth following the injuries, while pointing out they’re clearly the best team in the NFL so far.

“The 49ers are held together at times by Band-Aids and gauze tape, but there’s no question they’re the best team in football a third of the way through the season,” Vacciano wrote. “They need a rest, especially after WR Mike Evans reinjured his Achilles on Monday night, joining WR Deebo Samuel, WR Christian Kirk, edge rusher Nick Bosa and more on the sideline.

“But they’re so deep and so good, they can sleepwalk through wins — like they seemed to do at times in the second half Monday night when they nearly blew their game against the Commanders. Now they just have to get through Atlanta to hit their bye week undefeated and see if they can get some of their walking wounded back after that.

The Niners will be favored again this week on the road against the Atlanta Falcons, giving them a chance to go 7-0 entering their bye week, where they can get healthier and acquire reinforcements through the trade market. So far, so good here for San Francisco.

item.title: Dan Campbell hints at who will play alongside Brian Branch at safety
item.description: The Detroit Lions face an interesting decision on who plays alongside Brian Branch at safety.
item.content:encoded:
We now know that the Detroit Lions plan to play Brian Branch this week against the Green Bay Packers, marking the end of his 10+ month rehab after tearing his Achilles last season. Branch could make an immediate impact on the Lions’ struggling secondary, but Detroit’s coaching staff still has some decisions to make in terms of personnel.

The biggest question is simply: who is going to play alongside Branch? The Lions have gone through a litany of safeties this year, both due to injury and poor play. Avonte Maddox is out for the year with an injury, and Thomas Harper is on injured reserve for the foreseeable future. Meanwhile, the Lions have given significant playing time to Chuck Clark, Christian Izien, and recently rookie Keith Abney.

I asked Campbell what he’s looking for besides Branch, and the Lions coach mentioned that Branch is such a good, versatile player, that they can put any type of player alongside him, and the Pro Bowl player will make it work.

“Here’s what’s great about getting BB [Branch] back. BB gives you the flexibility is what do you want to do with anybody else?” Campbell said. “Because there are things you’re going to want to do with BB, high, let him play top down, and then there are things you want him to play underneath. And that doesn’t require somebody else playing off of him necessarily. He’ll make it right.”

On the surface, veteran Chuck Clark is a better player in the box given his physical limitation at age 32. Abney, while still very new to the position, is an athletic, rangey defender that could play some single-high looks.

Unsurprisingly, because the Lions view Branch as capable to fill both roles, Campbell expects to play both Clark and Abney against the Packers this week.

“We’re going to use all those guys,” Campbell said. “Chuck has been really steady for us, man. He’s smart veteran guy. He’s going to be where he’s supposed to be. And then I mentioned this about Abney. Abney is worth continuing to invest in. I mean, he’s going to play for us.”

Last game, both Abney and Clark were essential in utilizing a game plan to take away Arizona’s top two threat, Michael Wilson and Trey McBride. Detroit faces a much bigger threat in the passing game this week against the Green Bay Packers, and it’ll require an entirely different game plan.

Campbell described their options as “pick your poison.” The Packers have two deep-ball threats in receivers Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. But if your plan is to take the top away from both players, Green Bay can punish you over the middle with their Pro Bowl tight end Tucker Kraft.

“That’s the danger in it. Wherever you’re having to use some resources, then now you have got to worry about Kraft.” Campbell said. “If you’re going to use it to take the top off on some of this, well now you have got Kraft underneath and you have got to worry about the backs. It does, it creates some issues, man, that you have got to be ready for. And some of it is you better pick your poison. You can’t defend all of it, so you better pick your poison and what you think means the most to you to stop.”

Branch could very well be the antidote to Green Bay’s poison this week, but he’ll need help from everyone around him to make the entire defense work in harmony.

item.title: Can Robert Saleh’s defense continue leading Titans to victory?
item.description: The Tennessee Titans defense is finally starting to take shape under Robert Saleh
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans finally won a football game in Week 6, defeating the Indianapolis Colts 26-20. Robert Saleh’s defense undeniably powered the Nashville-based club to victory. The question goes begging, can Saleh’s defense continue carrying the Titans?

Saleh’s defense forced three turnovers through an Amani Hooker interception, a Jeffery Simmons strip, and a Cor’Dale Flott interception. Flott’s INT was the perfect example of Saleh’s scheme beginning to pay dividends. The cover-man passed off a Colts receiver smoothly and stepped in front of an ill-advised Jones throw.

The Titans also forced a fourth turnover via special teams. James Williams Sr. and Julius Chestnut combined to block a fourth-quarter punt. It was scooped up by Femi Oladejo and returned for a 14-yard touchdown that completed the comeback, making it 20 unanswered points in a then 20-13 Titans lead. They never trailed again.

Simmons sacked Jones twice. So did Jermaine Johnson II. Tony Adams and Jacob Martin contributed one sack apiece to round out the Titans’ six sacks.

Saleh’s defense covered for another mediocre offensive performance. Quarterback Cam Ward was 11-of-22 for 102 yards, one touchdown, and one interception. The Titans began three second-half offensive possessions from Colts territory. The offense only scored one touchdown. Brian Daboll’s unit was outgained 399-186.

Despite being 1-5, the Titans are now allowing the 13th-fewest points per game. They are tied for ninth in sacks despite lacking elite defensive line talent outside of Jeffery Simmons. You’re really beginning to see the Saleh defense come together.

Saleh’s defense will receive another opportunity to spearhead a victory versus a rather average Cleveland Browns offense in Week 7. The Browns are playing excellent on defense, so we probably shouldn’t expect the Titans offense to get on track against this opponent. No, it’ll take another big-time showing from Saleh’s unit to execute an upset.

item.title: 3 storylines for Giants vs. Texans: Will it be Jameis or J.J. at QB?
item.description: The quarterback decision is the big story this week, but it is hardly the only one.,
item.content:encoded:
The biggest storyline of the week heading into the New York Giants Week 7 game vs. the Houston Texans is whether the Giants will start Jameis Winston or J.J. McCarthy at quarterback.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh wasn’t ready to decide on Sunday night after McCarthy’s fourth-quarter heroics nearly brought the Giants back from a 24-point deficit in a 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints. On Monday, he said the team was still “honing in” on a decision.

Theoretically, Harbaugh does not have to announce a decision on Wednesday. It would seem logical, though, since this is the beginning of the practice week and reporters will see which quarterback takes the first reps during individual drills early in practice.

Fans who voted in our ‘Jameis or J.J.?’ poll clearly want McCarthy to start.

Do the Giants stay with Winston’s experience and his knowledge of the offense? It is a frustrating ride with Winston, but the Giants have lost one time in his four starts this season, and as a captain and member of the team’s Leadership Council, it is clear how much respect his teammates have for him.

Do they venture into the unknown with McCarthy, and perhaps risk upsetting what has thus far been a mostly harmonious locker room? McCarthy gives them mobility that allows them to expand their playbook, and maybe untapped upside at just 23 years of age. Still, it is important to remember that despite his impressive relief performance on Sunday, the Giants were able to get McCarthy because a team with a shaky quarterback situation had him as QB3 and was happy to be rid of him.

Getting going on the ground

The Giants’ offense was built to be a physical, run-first attack that would take some pressure off quarterback Jaxson Dart and wear down opposing defenses. Unfortunately, the Giants have not run the ball well. They average 3.8 yards per attempt, 22nd in the league. That number isn’t even a true picture of how ineffective the run game has been. It is inflated by a 28-yard J.J. McCarthy scramble, a 22-yard Dart run, and a 20-yard Darnell Mooney reverse.

The Giants do not have a 20-yard run from a running back this season. They average 3.9 yards per attempt when giving the ball to a back, with Cam Skattebo’s 3.6 yards per rush topping the list.

The backs and the blocking have both been problematic. Getting more production out of the run game is a must, and part of the Winston-McCarthy equation.

The backs

Harbaugh said the other day that he would love to have a Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley circumstance, with a clear No. 1 stud running back. Hopefully, nobody reminds Harbaugh that one of those guys was a Giant.

Go back to the offseason. The Giants were interested in free agent running back Kenneth Walker before he signed with the Kansas City Chiefs. They were thought to be seriously considering using the No. 5 overall pick on running back Jerimiyah Love.

It is clear they felt they needed more at running back. It is why they took a chance with Harris, a four-time 1,000-yard rusher. That didn’t pan out. quarterback situation had him as QB3 and was happy to be rid of him.

Skattebo is more bulldozer than big-play, breakaway back. With four fumbles in five games (the sixth doesn’t count since he never touched the ball), he has clearly lost some trust.

Tracy is a slasher and a good pass receiver. Of the current backs the Giants have, trying to get him more carries might be the Giants’ best chance to create more explosive runs. We know they need them:

Singletary is Mr. Consistency. He won’t make mistakes as a pass protector, and he has just four fumbles in 1,352 career touches. Going forward, it won’t surprise me if Singletary becomes the back the Giants close games with while trying to protect a lead.

The blocking

Watch the Giants try to run the football, and you too often see a block that doesn’t get executed. Harris’s 6-yard loss Sunday against the New Orleans Saints was a perfect example. He lost those yards because Jon Runyan Jr. got knocked into him about 4 yards behind the line of scrimmage. Harris had no chance on the play.

Pro Football Focus grades and Pro Football and Sports Network Impact scores are not perfect indicators of performance. But they can tell us some things.

An average PFF grade is 60.0. The Giants’ team run-blocking grade is 49.5, 29th in the league.

Only one regular player, right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (83.9), has been well above average as a run blocker. Fullback Patrick Ricard (55.6) and offensive linemen Runnyan (54.3), John Michael Schmitz (50.5), and Sisi Mauigoa (50.0) have been below average. Marcus Mbow is at 45.2 in limited duty.

An average PFSN Impact Score is 75.0. The Giants’ team run-blocking score is 69.0, 26th.

Only Giants’ offensive linemen have played enough snaps to qualify for a PFSN Impact Score. In run-blocking, Andrew Thomas (78.6) and Eluemunor (77.2) are slightly above average. Mauigoa 67.8) and Runyan (63.7) are well below average.

Mauigoa is having a rocky start to his career. Runyan is an excellent pass blocker, but a poor run blocker. Thomas is playing hurt. Eluemunor is now hurt. Bryan Hudson has replaced Schmitz at center, and it is too early to tell whether or not he is the answer at center.

Blame whoever and whatever you want, but too often Giants’ running backs have had no chance.

Beating themselves

The Giants are a team that does not have a huge margin for error. Four of their five games this season have been either one-score games or decided in the closing seconds.

The Giants have two victories courtesy of game-saving interceptions by Jevon Holland and Deonte Banks. Unfortunately, the Giants have a tie and a loss in the last two weeks that their own mistakes are to blame for.

Over six games, the Giants have actually made a shocking number of self-inflicted, sometimes undisciplined mistakes.

The Giants have fumbled 11 times. Only the Los Angeles Rams (13) have more fumbles. The Giants have lost seven of those fumbles. Add in four interceptions thrown by Giants quarterbacks, and New York has 11 turnovers. Only five teams have more. Overall, the Giants are -2 in takeaway/giveaway ratio.

Penalties have also been a problem. The Giants have 46, and only 11 teams have more. Twenty-four of those penalties have been pre-snap. Only the Cleveland Browns (29) have more pre-snap infractions.

The Giants have only five special teams penalties, the fifth-fewest in the NFL. Unfortunately, four of those came last week in the second half against the Saints. Those penalties negated punt returns by Charlie Jones of 32, 15, 33, and 9 yards.

Beating themselves is something the Giants have to stop doing.

item.title: Deep dive on Jets rookie Omar Cooper Jr.'s breakout game against Patriots
item.description: Jets wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. had a breakout game against the Patriots in Week 5. Here's a deep dive into what made the rookie so effective...
item.content:encoded:
Jets rookie Omar Cooper Jr. made his return from IR during Sunday's game against the Patriots in New England, and his impact was immediate.

Cooper, who caught just one pass in his NFL debut five weeks ago before suffering a high ankle sprain, caught six passes for 103 yards and a touchdown in his first extensive action. What does this performance tell us about the kind of player Cooper is going to develop into and how he fits in the Jets' offense?

Let’s break down the key plays in Cooper's performance...

1st quarter, 8:34 to go – 3rd and 10 at the Patriots' 14, no score

Cooper's first catch should have been an opening drive touchdown, but Tim Patrick was called for offensive pass interference in a situation where such a call isn't always made.

On the play, the Jets had four wide receivers with Cooper isolated on the right-hand side. As the play got extended and Geno Smith rolled left to buy time, Cooper ran across the field and found an open area near the goal line, showcasing his instincts and ability to read coverages.

2nd quarter, 10:15 to go – 1st and 10 at the Jets' 17, Patriots leading 7-3

Offensive coordinator Frank Reich has been criticized in some circles for not using enough pre-snap motion. However, with Cooper back, this could be something the Jets explore more often.

On this play, the Jets had two tight ends on the right side and Cooper was motioning in that direction before reversing course and coming back the other way. He released outside Garrett Wilson on the left side but then ran a deep crosser. Smith hit him coming across the middle where he made a tough 19-yard catch with a defender on his back.

3rd quarter, 10:32 to go – 1st and 10 at the Patriots' 48, Patriots leading 17-3

This was Cooper's big breakout moment, as his 48-yard touchdown got the Jets back into the game on a deep throw by Smith, which he actually had to wait for because it was underthrown and late.

Once again, how Cooper got open had more to do with his instincts than his route-running technique, as he split the safeties down the middle of the field, adjusting his route well to get behind the defense.

OMAR COOPER JR. 🔥 Geno Smith finds the rook for a 48-yard touchdown 🚀 https://t.co/QNp6swHTJ5

— SNY Jets (@snyjets) October 18, 2026

A key point is that Cooper was lined up incorrectly and should have been called for an illegal formation penalty, which would have negated the touchdown and demoralized the Jets in the middle of their comeback bid.

The Jets have had a handful of young receivers who haven't reached their potential due to errors such as this, including Denzel Mims, Malachi Corley, and Arian Smith. Receivers coach Shawn Jefferson must re-emphasize the details with Cooper because a penalty there could have turned the game into a much more comfortable win for the Patriots.

4th quarter, 1:08 to go – 1st and 10 at the Jets' 25, Patriots leading 26-16

The game was basically over at this stage, but the Jets connected with Cooper on a perfect drive-starter. The drive eventually led to a field goal, making it a one-score game and the Jets attempted an onside kick, which they almost recovered. Also, on an individual note, this secured the first 100-yard receiving game of the rookie's career.

With four wide receivers in the formation, Cooper took a screen pass in the slot and followed good blocks by Mason Taylor and Olu Fashanu to gain 18 yards. This was the only chance Cooper had to display his abilities after the catch, although we already caught a glimpse of his potential on his big catch-and-run in Week 1, so the Jets should look for him regularly on plays like this.

Aside from the four plays mentioned above, Cooper had three shorter catches, none of which went for a first down. However, that underlines how the Jets may look to get the ball in Cooper's hands underneath and rely on his playmaking ability to generate yardage.

***

Cooper's production in this game was excellent, and he showcased some of the skills he brings to the table. With Wilson having such a strong start to the season, defenses will invariably devote more attention to him, giving players like Cooper a chance to exploit matchup advantages. If Cooper continues to perform this way, it might even help to free up Wilson somewhat.

The Jets have AD Mitchell set to return from injury at some point soon, but this shouldn't affect Cooper's role. Patrick played 43 snaps in Sunday's game and only caught one pass, so Mitchell will most likely take over his workload, with Cooper continuing to play primarily in the slot but occasionally outside.

Three weeks ago, the Jets saw another first-round rookie -- tight end Kenyon Sadiq -- break out in similar fashion with a 100-yard game. However, his momentum has stalled since then. With a couple of winnable games coming up, Cooper can help the Jets get their season on track if he can build on this positive start.

item.title: Besides 3rd-down issues, the Cowboys defense had some success
item.description: Do you feel like the Cowboys defense has made any progress at all over the last few weeks?
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys didn’t have what it took to leave Lambeau with the win on Sunday night, falling to the Green Bay Packers, 23-13. While the loss is unpleasant, there were some things we can come out of this game and feel better about. Oddly enough, they’re on the defensive side of the ball.

Initially, it was frustrating for the Cowboys defense. They made some great plays on first down, often creating 2nd-and-10 or longer situations, and they would hold up okay on second down. But then, the bottom fell out. Again and again, the defense buckled on the money down, allowing the Packers to convert on third down. It was a total breakdown, and it just kept happening.

But they did get better as the game went on. The defense allowed the Packers to convert 9/10 on third down in the first half, but that dropped to just 2/8 in the second half. That’s a significant improvement.

While they struggled getting off the field in the first half, the defense as a whole did well in many areas. Their run defense was great. Granted, the Packers are one of the worst run offenses in the league, but the Cowboys shut them down. Even in a favorable game script for them, Green Bay only finished with 57 total rushing yards, and averaged just 2.2 yards per carry.

Quinnen Williams was overpowering blockers and shutting down rushing lanes. He and Kenny Clark controlled the interior of the trenches, and both came away with a sack, as did fellow defensive tackle Elijah Garcia. All three of these sacks were aided by pressure created by Rashan Gary. Overall, the pressure from the defensive front was good at times, but when they sent more defenders at Love, he usually found a wide-open target somewhere.

Dee Winters came away with the defensive play of the game with the team’s lone interception of the year. He was brought over to Dallas for his coverage ability, and it was nice to see it finally pay off. It’s a shame he was touched, a pick-six could have shifted the momentum a bit. The Cowboys offense then gave the ball right back shortly thereafter.

Speaking of coverage, it’s hard not to be pleased with what Joey Porter Jr. has given the team so far. Not only did this no-tackling corner make a great tackle right out of the gate, but he did what he’s touted to do, which is provide smothering coverage and break up passes. He did both of those things.

Even Malachi Lawrence showed some unexpected coverage skills by getting downfield and having the ball slightly graze off his hands just enough to cause an incompletion in the end zone. Whether it’s Porter Jr. or Lawrence, that’s two last-second deflections that saved a touchdown.

The Cowboys’ improvement resulted in allowing just six points in the second half, and 23 points total. That’s pretty decent. In the second half, the Packers had five drives and two of them resulted in field goals, and one of those happened when Green Bay started in Cowboys territory after the Dallas offense turned the ball over on downs. The other three drives the Packers had resulted in a net yardage total of just five yards. Two of those drives were three-and-outs and netted negative yards. That’s a great second-half showing.

There were certainly a lot of plays the defense wishes they could have back, but this group also made more impact plays in this game than we’ve seen in a while. There was a more all-hands-on-deck feel as more players were helping out in the run game, and Porter Jr.‘s play finally gave them some much-needed support in coverage. It was definitely something to build off of going forward.

item.title: Broncos at Cardinals preview: Denver aims for three-game win streak
item.description: The Broncos are coming off a big win over Seattle and the mini-bye for their game against the Cardinals on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos are coming off a huge win over the defending Super Bowl champs.

Next on the docket is a scrappy Arizona Cardinals bunch that just pulled a huge road upset of the Los Angeles Rams. The good news for the Broncos (4-2) is that they got the mini-bye week before heading to the desert and could get a few players back from injury and the commissioner’s exempt list.

Denver looks to extend its winning streak to three games after coming out of a gauntlet to start the season. The Broncos are currently -4.5-point road favorites over Arizona (2-4). The total sits at over/under 43.5 points, with a lean toward the over at -115.

Offensive Rankings 

Denver: Thirty-first in total offense (252.2 yards per game), 26th in rushing offense (84.2 YPG), 28th in passing offense (168.0 YPG), 26th in scoring offense (19.0 points per game).

Arizona: Twenty-third in total offense (307.3 yards per game), 22nd in rushing offense (96.3 YPG), 20th in passing offense (211.0 YPG), 24th in scoring offense (21.0 points per game).

Defensive Rankings   

Denver: Twenty-second in total defense (348.3 yards per game), 31st in rushing defense (139.8 YPG), 10th in passing defense (208.5 YPG), tied for 10th in scoring defense (20.8 points per game).

Arizona: Twenty-third in total defense (350.5 yards per game), 20th in rushing defense (120.8 YPG), 22nd in passing defense (229.7 YPG), tied for 31st in scoring defense (29.7 points per game).

Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Sunday’s game.

Win the line of scrimmage on offense

The Broncos offensive line has been the definition of “meh” to start the regular season. It’s nowhere near what it’s been the last few seasons, but it also isn’t horrid either. Denver needs to dominate the line of scrimmage on Sunday. Open lanes in the running game and do a better job of pass protection. It’s a cliche, but success on offense starts in the trenches. Getting that could lay the foundation for jump-starting the offense. — Ian St. Clair

Bench Bo Nix; Start Jarrett Stidham

Just kidding. Ya’ll crazy if you think benching Bo Nix is even remotely the answer. That said, Bo Nix does need to play better, and he isn’t seeing the field well to start the season. He’s had slow starts in every season he’s played, so, for now, I’m chalking this up to another slow start. However, seven games in, I’m hoping to see him take flight a bit now that the hardest part of the Broncos’ schedule is complete. At 4-2, they got through it with a winning record, and that is all we could hope for. — Tim Lynch

Pressure the QB

The key to this game is the same as it has been every week. Get to the QB. The defense has done a great job this season of causing mayhem in the backfield. Make it uncomfortable for Jacoby Brissett (like the back of a Volkswagen). When QBs are harassed and hurried, they make mistakes. — Adam Malnati

Disciplined, execution-based offensive football

This team needs to execute at a high level, and it will win this game easily. The defense is already there. If the offense can up its game, this Broncos team will be unstoppable. — Sadaraine

Limit the impact of Trey McBride

The Broncos defense has performed well this season, aside from a few games. For the most part, they’ve been able to limit the impact of the opposing team’s top player on their offense. This week, they face All-Pro tight end Trey McBride, who is coming off a sensational 2025 season. He is the focal point of Arizona’s aerial attack and gets over ten targets per game. Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph needs to come up with a good game plan that limits his impact on the game. If they can slow him down, Denver will have a great shot at earning their fifth victory of the season. — Christopher Hart

Teams: Syracuse Orange (2-4, 0-4) at North Carolina Tar Heels (4-2, 2-1)

TV/Streaming: ACC Network, WatchESPN

Radio: Cuse.com, TK 99/105, WAER 88.3, SiriusXM 258

Rivalry: 5-3, UNC

Current Streak: 3, UNC

First Meeting: If you forgot how long former UNC Head Coach Mack Brown has been around college football, let this be a reminder. The 20th-ranked Tar Heels began their 8th season during Brown’s first stint at Chapel Hill in 1995 with a home game against Syracuse. There, a redshirt freshman by the name of Donovan McNabb led ‘Cuse to a 20-9 victory at Kenan Stadium. Whatever happened to him?

Last Meeting: The last game that these teams played was last year in the JMA Wireless Dome. That game featured the surprise start of Joseph Filardi at quarterback for the Orange. Syracuse only managed 152 yards of total offense that day as UNC won 27-10.

Head Coaches: Syracuse: Fran Brown (third year, 15-16) | UNC: Bill Belichick (second year, 8-10)

Coach Bio: Belichick was raised in Annapolis, Maryland. His dad, Steve, was an assistant football coach at Navy. Bill attended Wesleyan University and played center and tight end on the football team. He also played lacrosse and squash in college.

Belichick started his coaching career as an assistant with the Baltimore Colts, Detroit Lions and Denver Broncos. His reputation grew with the New York Giants. He started as a defensive assistant and special teams coach with the Giants, eventually adding linebackers coaching to his role. Belichick would then be named defensive coordinator of New York in 1985 under head coach Bill Parcells. The Giants won two Super Bowls with Belichick as defensive coordinator.

His first head coaching job came with the Cleveland Browns. Belichick only had one winning season with the Browns and was fired after the Browns moved to Baltimore to become the Ravens. He rejoined Parcells with the New England Patriots for a season. Both moved to the New York Jets for three seasons. Parcells stepped down after the 1999 season and arranged for the Jets to hire Belichick as Jets head coach. But Belichick decided to join the New England Patriots instead as their head coach.

Belichick won six Super Bowls with the Patriots, all alongside Tom Brady. He finished his New England career with a 266-121 record. Belichick and the Patriots agreed to mutually part ways after the 2023 season. After a short media career, North Carolina hired Belichick as its head coach for the 2025 season.

Last Year: UNC struggled under Belichick in its first season. The Tar Heels only won two ACC games and stumbled to a 4-8 record. 

Last Game: UNC rang the Victory Bell last week as the Tar Heels won the Tobacco Road rivalry battle at Duke. The Tar Heels scored with 1:53 left in the 4th quarter to win 24-20 over the Blue Devils.

“Fear Me, I’ve Killed Hundreds of Timelords”: Remember this guy? Former Syracuse linebacker Derek McDonald transferred to UNC in the offseason. He leads the ACC in total tackles with 56 on the season.

If Syracuse Loses: If you haven’t already, start praying to your Gerry shrine

item.title: Dan Campbell: Packers offense will make plays, we have to make more
item.description: The Packers offense had some rocky moments in the opening weeks of the season, but the last two weeks have seen the unit find its footing.
item.content:encoded:
The Packers offense had some rocky moments in the opening weeks of the season, but the last two weeks have seen the unit find its footing.

They've put up 54 points and 746 yards while turning the ball over once in wins over the Bears and Cowboys that have them sitting at 4-2 ahead of Sunday's game in Detroit. The Lions defense had a good showing in its Week 5 game against the Cardinals and they'll be hoping that carries over through last week's bye, but head coach Dan Campbell isn't expecting the group to pitch a shutout.

Campbell called Packers quarterback Jordan Love the team's "secret sauce" during his Tuesday press conference and highlighted the touch he's thrown on deep balls to Christian Watson and Matthew Golden as a particular concern. The two wideouts have 59 catches for 1,039 yards and nine touchdowns on the season, which is why Campbell said the team needs to be prepared to win in a shootout if necessary.

“They’re going to make some plays, but it’s about us making more of ‘em,” Campbell said. “If we get an opportunity for something, we have got to make the most of it, something that swings in our favor. We have to capitalize on those.”

The Packers beat the Lions twice last season and extending that winning streak would push the Lions further into fourth place in a very competitive decision, so Campbell will have to make sure his team is sharp on both sides of the ball this weekend.

item.title: The Rams worked out 42-year old Matt Prater
item.description: The Los Angeles Rams worked our Matt Prater and other NFL news on a Wednesday
item.content:encoded:
Matt Prater is one of the best NFL kickers viewers have had the privilege to watch for years. He maybe almost joined the Los Angeles Rams. Now, Prater has been in the league since 2006 so with that longevity comes experience, but age. Age equating to diminished performance can be the end of an NFL career.

Prater specialized as a long-distance kicker with the most 50+ yard field goals made in NFL history. Prime Prater with Sean McVay would’ve been a cheat code for points. McVay did somewhat have this type of kicker with Greg Zuerlein, he was great when he was great, but Prater was a bit better.

All that aside, the Rams are going with Brandon McManus.

You could say I buried the lede down here, but how desperate are the Rams for a kicker?

Very desperate. As their dream turned nightmare season rolls along.

Brandon McManus is latest signing in Rams’ kicker carousel (clutchpoints)

“The Los Angeles Rams are signing veteran kicker Brandon McManus, their third kicker of the 2026 NFL season.

The move follows Blake Grupe’s torn ACL during Sunday’s 18-16 loss to the Arizona Cardinals at SoFi Stadium.

McManus, 35, worked out Tuesday alongside free-agent kicker Matt Prater as Los Angeles addressed its special-teams problems.

The Rams are 2-4 after six games and hope the veteran can bring stability to the position.

NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport shared details of the agreement Tuesday on X, formerly Twitter, citing information gathered alongside fellow insider Mike Garafolo.“

NFC West standings: Rams fall to last place, 4 games behind 49ers (ramswire)

“It doesn’t help that the Rams have already lost to the 49ers, too, so they can’t sweep San Francisco and clinch that tiebreaker in the event that they finish with the same record. They’ll have to finish with a better divisional record than the 49ers in that case, which seems unlikely considering San Francisco is 3-0 and the Rams are 0-2.

The Rams have to go on a run before their Week 11 bye. They’ve got four winnable games coming up, one of which is a rematch against the Cardinals in Week 10. Their other opponents are the Raiders, Chargers and Commanders, who are all at or below .500.“

Past NFC Champ Takes Swipe at Rams for Losing to Mike LaFleur, Cardinals (heavy.com)

“Cardinals veteran wide receiver Kendrick Bourne blasted LA via Instagram in a post that surfaced after the 18-16 victory.

He believes the Rams haven’t looked efficient on offense without LaFleur there.

“Them boys ain’t the same wit out LaFleur,” Bourne posted on his personal IG page.

LaFleur worked under McVay as offensive coordinator before accepting the Cardinals head coaching opening in the 2026 offseason. He became the latest past McVay OC to land a head coaching gig; following the path of brother Matt LaFleur, Zac Taylor, and Kevin O’Connell. The latter three have guided playoff runs or, in the case of the Cincinnati Bengals head coach Taylor, a Super Bowl appearance against the Rams in 2021.“

Rams put 2 players on IR, officially sign new kicker (ramswire)

“The Los Angeles Rams made a trio of roster moves on Tuesday, all of which were expected. They placed Davante Adams and Poona Ford on injured reserve and signed kicker Brandon McManus to replace Blake Grupe.

Interestingly, they did not put Kobie Turner on IR yet, though Sean McVay said on Monday that the team will likely move him there at some point; he’s expected to miss a “handful of weeks,” as McVay put it.

Adams will be out 6-10 weeks with a ruptured hamstring, while Ford will miss the rest of the season with a torn triceps. Turner injured his groin in Sunday’s loss but McVay didn’t have an exact timetable for his return.“

Rams are gambling on Brandon McManus being past his Packers collapse (ramblinfan)

“Last season, McManus ranked 43rd out 43 kickers as measured by FanSided’s Kick Value Added metric. he names directly above him? Ironically enough, LA’s Joshua Karty and Grupe. 

Hopefully McManus can keep those gargoyles at bay for as long as the Rams must rely on him. 

Brandon McManus isn’t dependable, but he’ll have to do for the Rams

McManus did, at least, beat out an ancient Matt Prater in Tuesday’s audition. If you’re looking for more robust reassurance, well, there really isn’t any, but McManus was highly effective in 2024, his first Packers season.“

NFL Power Rankings Week 7: Rams Fall 12 Spots, Steelers Up 5 (nfl.com)

“Check out Nick Shook’s Power Rankings for Week 7 of the 2026 NFL Season.”

49ers fans can laugh at the Rams (but it would be foolish to count them out) (ninernoise)

“While it is more than fair, and probably even encouraged, to laugh at the Rams right now, it would be silly to count them out entirely. Yes, they have been really bad and have had some key injuries, but they still have a lot of talent on the roster, and it would be surprising if head coach Sean McVay isn’t able to figure something out by the end of the season.

The Myles Garrett trade has not worked out as planned, and Davante Adams is going to be out for a while. But the Rams’ upcoming schedule is not especially scary, and if they get some of their guys back late in the season and start to peak for the playoffs, then they will definitely be a team no one wants to face in the playoffs.“

Jaguars could gift LA Rams a WR spark with Brian Thomas Jr. trade (blackandteal)

“The Washington Commanders most definitely make sense because of Thomas’ LSU connection with quarterback Jayden Daniels. However, there’s another club in the NFC that would make a push for him.

The Jaguars could trade Brian Thomas Jr. to the LA Rams in return for a 2nd-round pick

Like other teams that are dealing with injuries at receiver, Los Angeles would be a realistic landing spot for Brian Thomas Jr. While Puka Nacua is back in the fold after sitting out two contests with a groin and a core muscle injury, teammate Davante Adams will tentatively miss six to 10 games after sustaining a hamstring rupture. Brian Thomas Jr. would be a more than capable replacement, as Michel Haney at Ramblin Fan suggests. Here’s the skinny.“

5 things to know about new Rams kicker Brandon McManus (ramswire)

He’s a Super Bowl champion

Before the Broncos went on a decade-long playoff drought that lasted after McManus’ departure, he won Super Bowl 50 with the team. During that playoff run, McManus hit all 10 field goal attempts and was perfect in point-after attempts.“

Raiders Won’t Face Former Star Davante Adams as Rams Lose Key Players (sports.yahoo)

Sunday’s game would have marked his first appearance against the Raiders since leaving Las Vegas.

Adams had been one of the Rams’ most productive offensive players this season, catching 30 passes for 480 yards and four touchdowns through six games.

His absence is another significant setback for Los Angeles, which has struggled to a 2-4 start.“

item.title: 5 Lions vs. Packers thoughts after watching Green Bay’s win over Cowboys
item.description: A look at how the Green Bay Packers are playing lately, and what it means for the Detroit Lions this week.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions face off against the Green Bay Packers this week, and the timing could be tough for them. The Packers have shrugged off an ugly start to the season and are now riding a three-game winning streak. Their last two wins in particular—blowout wins over the Bears and Cowboys—have been impressive.

I watched the Packers’ last game against the Cowboys, both live and again on replay, and took some notes as it may pertain to this week’s game against the Lions.

Packers have no run game

Green Bay let the Cowboys hang around for much longer than they should have, and a lot of that has to do with their lack of a running game. The Packers scored just six second-half points against a terrible Cowboys defense. Removing two Jordan Love kneel-downs, the Packers rushed for just 42 yards on 17 carries in the second half (2.57 YPC). Mind you, this is a Cowboys defense that, even after this performance, ranks dead last in rushing yards allowed (149.8 per game) and 25th in DVOA.

For the season, Green Bay is dead last in:

  • Rushing yards per game (59.8)
  • Yards per carry (2.9)
  • Rush EPA (-0.299)
  • 31st in rushing success rate (32.5%)

Green Bay will likely get Josh Jacobs back this week, which should help. But there are systemic issues with their running game, including a busted offensive line. If recently added guard Kevin Zeitler makes his first appearance this week, it could have a bigger impact than Jacobs’ return.

Green Bay’s safeties are awesome and versatile

Watching the Packers deploy Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams in creative and exciting ways made me yearn for the days of a healthy Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph. Both players are so versatile, and defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has done an awesome job putting them in positions to make plays. Just watch him hide Williams close to the line, only to have him back out, scream to the opposite side of the field, and pick off a completely unsuspecting Dak Prescott.

For the season, the duo has a combined five interceptions, 2.0 sacks, six quarterback hits, and 73 tackles.

They will stress both Jared Goff and the Lions’ receivers, making it hard to both attack the deep portion of the field (GB is 11th in EPA per pass on deep balls) and the middle of the field (first in EPA per pass against slot targets). This will put more pressure on Detroit’s boundary receivers to win against what is a pretty mediocre cornerback group in Green Bay.

Deep ball merchants

While Anthony Balaj put together a nice piece on why the Packers’ deep-ball game may not be as threatening as it seems, it’s still a huge part of what the Packers do on offense. Though Love didn’t connect on a deep shot against the Cowboys, they did benefit from a 37-yard pass interference penalty on a deep shot to Bo Melton. In fact, no one in the NFL has benefited more from defensive pass interference penalties than the Packers through six games, with a league-leading 135 yards gained.

No team has more passing attempts of 20+ air yards than the Packers (5.3 per game), although their +0.32 EPA per deep shot only ranks them 19th in the NFL.

Meanwhile, the Lions have been horrible against deep shots this year. They’re dead last in EPA/pass (+1.41) and are giving up the second-most yards per game (80.6) on deep shots. Detroit is hoping the return of Brian Branch this week may help stabilize the back end, but this may be their biggest test of the season.

Careful blitzing Jordan Love

Dallas tried to bring some extra pressure to test a poor Packers offensive line, but Jordan Love had all of the answers before the Cowboys could get home. While Dallas was able to produce a 53.8% pressure rate on those blitzes (eighth-highest of Week 8), Love still torched them on those plays. He went 8-for-12 for 100 yards and one sack against the blitz. He produced the sixth-highest yards per attempt (8.4) and second-highest EPA/dropback (+0.43) against the blitz in Week 6.

His season-long stats are a little more tame, ranking 13th in EPA/dropback (+0.03), 12th in yards per attempt (8.1), and 11th in passer rating (104.2) against the blitz.

Still, if I were the Lions, I would test my luck trying to create pressure without deploying extra defenders. Love’s statistics are actually much worse with no blitz, ranking:

  • 23rd in passer rating (84.4)
  • 17th in yards per attempt (7.1)
  • 17th in EPA/dropback (+0.05)

Given that the Lions are producing the seventh-highest pressure rate without blitzing (35.5%) and the Packers are allowing the sixth-highest pressure rate on non-blitz plays (36.2%), the game plan seems obvious.

Well-coached blitzing

The Packers dialed up some well-timed and well-disguised blitzes against Dallas that ensured a comeback attempt from the Cowboys never came close to materializing. In total, they had a 35.7% blitz rate (11th-highest of the week). More importantly, it was effective. On blitzes, they were able to produce a 45.0% pressure rate (13th), and it completely disrupted Dak Prescott and what was one of the best passing offenses in the league. Against the blitz, Dak Prescott was just 12-of-20 passing for 79 yards (4.0 yards per attempt — ranking 28 out of 29 qualifying QBs in Week 6).

Detroit’s offensive line has been better than expected this year, but the reshuffled unit is still figuring things out when it comes to handling the blitz, allowing the third-highest time to pressure in the NFL against the blitz (2.21 seconds). Thankfully, Jared Goff tends to make things right by getting the ball out quickly and avoiding the negative plays. Despite the quick pressure, Detroit still has the second-highest EPA per pass against the blitz (+0.33).

item.title: 1 playoff win, 10 seasons, and 100 reasons why the Colts had to fire Chris Ballard
item.description: It was a long time coming.
item.content:encoded:
“I don’t understand how that person still works here.”

That is a statement most of us have made at some time or another about that one person who seems to get away with everything despite their poor performance. They’re late. They don’t get all their work done. Others have to pick up the slack, and they have a bad attitude. Somehow, they keep their job. It’s as if they have something on the boss… When the day finally comes and that person has been released or left, it’s almost unbelievable even though you’ve anticipated it for years. That is exactly how I feel about the Indianapolis Colts finally pulling the trigger and firing Chris Ballard.

For the last three years, I have publicly advocated for the Colts to cut ties with Ballard. It’s nothing personal. It’s just business, and business has been bad. It was bad enough to justify a firing before the last three years, but a bad thing has somehow gotten worse. Ballard had some bright spots. This isn’t to say everything he touched turned to dust, but in the NFL, a few bright spots don’t cut it. Winning is all that matters and quite frankly, Ballard didn’t do enough of it.

To the Ballard apologists, we can look historically or recently, but the outlook doesn’t change. After ten years at the helm, Ballard’s Colts made the playoffs twice, winning once. They have zero AFC championships during that time. A hat with AFC South Champs would have been in the Goodwill bin during the Manning years because they were a dime a dozen. Nowadays, they would be like discovering buried treasure. 

Why didn’t the Colts win under Ballard? I’ll give you a hint: it has nothing to do with Andrew Luck retiring. Was that a blow? Certainly, but life is all about how we handle adversity. Ballard had plenty of years and chances to right that ship. There were some fantastic draft picks along the way, but there were way too many failures too. Build the trenches was the motto, but the modern NFL is built on the edges and at quarterback. Even the trenches have struggled mightily over the years. A fresh and more modern approach is needed.

If you don’t like history, let’s look at this year. A 2-4 record after having lost to the worst team in football at home was the final straw. A $50 million quarterback who isn’t throwing downfield and when he does, it’s to the other team, and a benched fourth overall pick backing him up is the current situation at the game’s most important position. Receivers are being brought in off the street while the defensive line generates no pressure, resulting in the secondary getting cooked. This isn’t legacy. This is now. In a win now, what have you done for me lately type of league, this doesn’t cut it.  Pile on the last decade, and it’s obvious why the Colts cut ties.

Honestly, if you’re still on the fence about this move, why? What have you seen that makes you still back Chris Ballard? “Well, you can fire him but that doesn’t mean there is someone better to take his place…” Maybe that’s the case, but most likely not. Does it get much worse? Being too good to rebuild with quality draft selections but not good enough to be in contention is the worst possible place for a sports franchise. Ballard knew the gig was up. He knew he didn’t perform to the required standards, and the Colts were more than patient. There were 100 reasons to fire Ballard. It took the 100th, but the right move was finally made.

item.title: Ravens discussion: silver linings coming out of loss to Browns
item.description: Join today’s discussion about silver linings from the Ravens’ Week 6 loss to the Browns.
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens are 4-2 after their loss to the Cleveland Browns with a tough slate of opponents on the docket. Before we turn the page on Sunday’s game, let’s grab a few positives out of the defeat to take into Week 7.

Nikhil Mehta

Kyle Hamilton has been the Ravens’ primary nickel defender this year, but between his versatile deployment and Jesse Minter’s use of dime personnel, the team still needs a reliable slot corner. Second-year UDFA Keyon Martin won the job out of training camp, but was benched after an up-and-down Week 1 showing. Fifth-round rookie Chandler Rivers’ performance was even more of a rollercoaster, leading to Martin’s return in Week 6. He practically shut down one Browns drive on his own with a PBU and a sack, and he did not deserve the pass interference flag that set up Cleveland’s game-tying touchdown in the fourth quarter. Martin also downed a Ryan Eckley punt at the one-yard line.

Dustin Cox

The silver lining for me coming out of the Ravens’ loss to the Browns was the pass rush. Seeing Trey Hendrickson and Nnamdi Madubuike playing at a high level on the field together was an encouraging sign of what the pass rush can look like going forward. Getting Mike Green going at the same time as Hendrickson is the dilemma now, as both appear to be most effective rushing from the right side of the defense. Hendrickson and Madubuike are the two highly-paid stars up front, though, and they certainly played like it on Sunday with 11 pressures.

Zach Canter

My biggest silver linings was how well the defense played, only allowing 13 total points with five sacks and 10 quarterback hits, and the return of Ja’Kobi Lane. The defense only allowed one touchdown all day, which was practically gift wrapped to the Browns. A Derrick Henry fumble gave them possession at the Ravens 35 and then an excellent Keyon Martin 3rd down stop was inexplicably called a pass interference, giving the Browns the ball inside the 10 with a fresh set of downs. They were nails all game, until the final drive where a great play call from Cleveland’s head coach Todd Monken against Minter’s Tampa 2 put them in field goal range. While it sucks they gave up the final points, only allowing 13 is an excellent performance in today’s NFL.

Ja’Kobi Lane was another bright spot, finishing with 4 catches for 40 yards. The offseason hype machine was put on hold after an early Week 1 injury put Lane on IR for four weeks. But he came back and immediately showed himself as a quarterback friendly target with the hands that made him special. Hopefully we’ll get to see some highlight reel plays downfield thrown from Lamar Jackson soon.

Frank Platko

A silver lining from the Ravens’ defeat in Week 6 was the performance of rookie pass-catchers Ja’Kobi Lane and Josh Cuevas. Lane was essentially making his season debut again having only played the first half of Week 1 and made an immediate impact. He made four catches for first down conversions and looked comfortable over the middle of the field as a space-eater. Lane should be a fixture in the passing game from here on out. Cuevas took on an elevated role with Matthew Hibner sidelined and had a season-best performance. He caught four passes for 44 yards, with a long 29-yard snag and fourth-down touchdown as well. With Mark Andrews on a declining trajectory and Durham Smythe out for the year, the Ravens will need their young tight ends to quickly acclimate into big roles. Cuevas showed a lot of promise against the Browns as a receiving threat moving forward.

item.title: Week 6, 3 Up and 3 Down: standout performances on both sides of the spectrum
item.description: Kyle Pitts was a standout, while the pass protection must improve.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Falcons fell behind early to the Chicago Bears and couldn’t recover. A late push created highlights for some, but a few obvious lowlights put them in the hole to begin with.

Here’s the Week 6, 3 up and 3 down.

3 up

Kyle Pitts

The tight end led the Falcons 4th-quarter resurgence with some fantastic individual efforts. For years, fans have complained about Pitts’ engagement, but this season he’s definitely played hard every snap regardless of the score. His YAC ability has flashed on limited touches, and he’s one of the team’s best answers for dealing with pressure.

Unfortunately, he just isn’t getting the looks, and he’s gotten opportunities only during mop-up duty. Pitts has earned the chance to be a priority; Tommy Rees and Michael Penix Jr. have to make it happen.

Jessie Bates III

Bates cracks the list two weeks in a row after forcing a fumble that helped turn the tide late in the game. A few weeks ago, Bates was in the down column due to him overextending himself too often, but he’s tightened up since then, and the play-making opportunities are coming his way.

Bates had a couple of nice run fits in the box and prevented anything from going over the top. Credit to Caleb Williams for executing the death-by-1000-paper-cuts strategy, but Bates did his job on Sunday.

Jared Ivey

Ivey played under 20 snaps, but he made the most of them. He finished as PFF’s highest-graded Falcons defender, and the film backs up that grade. He made multiple stops at and behind the line of scrimmage against the run and pressured Williams a handful of times. He can play from 3-tech to wide 9, making him a versatile depth piece, and while he is a noticeably stiff player, his hustle is undeniable. This game tied for his 2nd-greatest number of snaps for the season, and I wouldn’t be surprised to see a slight increase against the San Francisco 49ers.

3 down

Olamide Zaccheaus 

The WR had a brutal outing and was a constant negative for the Falcons offense. He’s been unreliable as a blocker and hasn’t given anyone a reason to trust him as a receiver. Among WRs who’ve run at least 50 routes in 2026, Zaccheaus has the second-worst Total EPA (-0.92) and EPA/Target (-0.08) per SumerSports.

He dropped a 3rd-down conversion on the game’s second drive and was later immediately accused by Michael Penix Jr. of giving up on his route. OZ was never cut out to be a WR3 this season, and it’s time to shrink his snaps.

Zachariah Branch

This performance hurt, mainly because it had nothing to do with his WR ability; he was positive in his very limited snaps. However, Branch has been inconsistent as a returner this year, and his two turnovers Sunday cost the Falcons big time.

The muff on punt team was partly due to a technique known as the “Banana Ball,” but the main issue is that he’s trying to field a punt inside the 10. OZ did the same thing when he was put in later, and that’s a massive red flag for this coaching staff. That said, you can’t turn the ball over. It was good to see the vets rally around Branch, but a break from return duties and more WR work might help. 

Pass Protection 

No one person or unit is responsible for the Falcons protection woes; they’re failing as a family. Penix has to get better at diagnosing the blitz pre-and-post-snap and work through his progression. Tommy Rees has to actually give Penix something to progress through. There’s a lack of answers in the short game, and some of these route concepts take too much time. The offensive line has to get better at passing off stunts from center to guard and from guard to tackle. They also need to be on the same page when navigating the blitz, especially Bijan Robinson, who struggled a lot with DBs this weekend. This will be the biggest issue for the offense until they prove they’ve learned from their mistakes.

Not the result fans or the team wanted, but the sky isn’t falling. You can’t turn the ball over on special teams; if those plays go the other way, we’re looking at a very different game. Pass protection is the biggest area of improvement, and Rees better figure it out because the 49ers defense is humming.

item.title: Dolphins news: Week 7 roster moves include addition of Zane Gonzalez, cut Storm Duck
item.description: A collection of Miami Dolphins news from around the web, including a look at the series of roster moves Miami made to start Week 7.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday was a busy day for the Miami Dolphins, with the front office making several roster moves. The Dolphins swapped kickers on Tuesday, bring back Zane Gonzalez and waiving Riley Patterson. Patterson was 7-for-0 on field goals this season and 5-for-6 on extra point attempts. After connecting on 93.1 percent of this field goal attempts, including 3-of-4 from over 50 yards, last year, Patterson’s accuracy seem to fall off this year, but a bigger issue seemed to be on kickoffs.

“We did try to kick them out of the end zone; that was discussed and just not executed the way that we wanted it to be…yeah, several of them were supposed to be touchbacks and weren’t,” head coach Jeff Hafley explained on Monday when asked about the team’s special teams issues and lack of simply kicking the ball for touchbacks rather than relying on the coverage unit.

The Dolphins held a tryout for kickers on Tuesday, including former seven-time Pro Bowl selection Justin Tucker, and ultimately brought back Gonzalez. The Cleveland Browns’ 2017 seventh-round draft pick, Gonzalez landed on injured reserve during the preseason with Miami this past summer. He was released with an injury settlement and now returns to to the Dolphins, signing with the practice squad.

Miami was not done with their roster moves. They also promoted rookie edge rusher Rodney McGraw from the practice squad and waived edge rusher Andre Jones Jr. The potentially surprise move of the day came with the news the Dolphins were waiving cornerback Storm Duck.

A 2024 undrafted free agent out of Louisville, Duck was on the physically unable to perform list this year as he recovered from a knee injury sustained last year. He returned to practice three weeks ago, and the team has until today to decide whether to add him to the active 53-man roster or keep him on the PUP for the rest of the year. Instead, Miami moved on from Duck.
